📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prepare for fellow guests to go back for seconds when you bring these editor-approved dishes to the function.

There’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests.

Granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options.

Below, the Eater staff chimed on a handful of our annual favorites.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Making this appetizer is kind of like making a giant sandwich (positive). The feuilleté is filled with layered, thin slices of ham, Swiss cheese, and Dijon mustard, and given a nice heavy cream-and-egg wash sheen. If I have time, I’ll head to my local cheese shop and see what Swiss varieties the mongers are excited about, but I also love the ease of using a pre-sliced cheese [assumes Sandra Lee voice] from the grocery store. My favorite is Sargento’s baby Swiss for its mild, nutty flavor and creamy texture. I should also mention that this appetizer is easy to transport; you can cut it into a million tiny squares if you’re attending a big party, or several larger squares if it’s a more intimate event. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

This is a bit of a project dish, perfect for a competitive friendsgiving or a cold weather potluck with a collection of amazing home cooks. Don’t skip the fried garlic breadcrumb topping, I think it completes this luscious macaroni and cheese. But I’ve also had plenty of friends adjust this recipe for picky family members, just using the incredible bechamel cheese sauce without all the herbs and garlic topping. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

Dirty martinis have never been dirtier or more ubiquitous (at least not in my elder millennial lifetime) and, like the Caesar, the briny, olive-y flavor has become a format that can be replicated in other edible forms. (Dirty martini deviled eggs, hello.) This dirty martini dip is a perennial fave for the savory snackers; it’s a classic cream-cheese-based party dip but with big flavor. I like it with ridged chips, like Ruffles. I always serve it at my annual holiday party to rave reviews. Would be incredible alongside a caviar service! — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Deb Perelman, Smitten Kitchen; Shilpa Uskokovic, Bon Appétit.

I love to cook, but I’m generally not much of a baker — I don’t generally have the patience for fiddly presentation or precise measurements, and given I lack a sweet tooth, there isn’t a ton of motivation for that to change. The one exception is bread, where I’ve steadily improved my game over the years, and I’ve found focaccia to be a welcome addition to any potluck. I have a standard recipe from a bread-making class that I tend to default to, but sometimes the occasion requires something more festive. In those instances, I turn to variations like this bagel-esque concoction from Smitten Kitchen (a great addition to any brunch spread), or this cacio e pepe twist from Bon Appétit, which adds a bit more zip and character to a standard focaccia recipe. And if you have less of an aversion to fiddly-ness than I do, just Google “decorative focaccia” to see how people much more artistic than I am fashion flowers from tomatoes, rosemary, and onion slices to top their breads — if you really want to show off. — Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

According to recent reports, back when I was deep in my potluck moment, a friend at a gathering once remarked, “You love a phyllo pie.” It was then that I sheepishly realized that I did, having brought one to several gatherings this friend had attended. There are many reasons for that. They travel well: You can pack the pie up still in the springform to provide support during the journey. They’re easy to prep: You can make the fillings ahead of time and assemble the day of. And they’re not very fussy when you arrive at your destination: Simply ask your host if you can pop it in the oven briefly, and at this time of year, you can almost always glom the warmth off something else that’s in there.

The recipe that set me off on this course came from Ottolenghi’s Shelf Love. It features cauliflower in a thick cheese sauce, making it perfect for the colder months when people want hearty food. I’ve found that the concept is welcoming to many different vegetables and all kinds of cheese; I’ve swapped in mushrooms and beans, or added caramelized onions or leeks, or taken liberties with Gruyère and greens. At gatherings with attendees who are vegan or lactose-intolerant, I’ve made them dairy-free (store-bought phyllo is generally vegan). In warmer months, or when I’d rather bring a skillet instead of a loaded springform, I opt for an approach to phyllo pie more like this spanakopita-esque recipe from Hetty McKinnon. But the format pairs well with many vegetables, and I always want to make sure to keep the vegetarians at the potluck well-fed. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Scientists Discover a Powerful Newly introduced Way To Kill Prostate Cancer Cells

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even prostate tumors resistant to standard treatments responded to an experimental molecule in animal studies, raising the possibility of a different approach to advanced disease.
  • Most cancer drugs work by blocking proteins or signaling pathways that help tumors grow.
  • The approach targets the androgen receptor (AR) and a helper protein called p300, which work together to activate genes that fuel prostate cancer growth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even prostate tumors resistant to standard treatments responded to an experimental molecule in animal studies, raising the possibility of a different approach to advanced disease.

Most cancer drugs work by blocking proteins or signaling pathways that help tumors grow. Researchers at the University of Michigan Health Rogel Cancer Center are testing a different approach. Instead of blocking two cancer-driving proteins separately, they have developed a molecule that locks them together, disrupting their activity and showing promising results against prostate cancer.

The approach targets the androgen receptor (AR) and a helper protein called p300, which work together to activate genes that fuel prostate cancer growth.

Sources indicate that “Our molecule acts like a molecular brace, connecting these two cancer-driving proteins in an abnormal configuration that traps them in an inactive state,” said senior study author Arul M. Chinnaiyan, MD, PhD, director of the Michigan Center for Translational Pathology and S.P. Hicks Professor of Pathology at Michigan Medicine.

“This shuts down two oncogenic signaling pathways simultaneously, enabling highly effective killing of tumor cells while sparing normal cells. Our preclinical findings suggest that this approach could offer a more effective treatment strategy for prostate cancer,” Chinnaiyan remarked.

According to recent reports, the researchers call the approach DALTAC, short for domain-alteration chimeras. It builds on a growing field known as chemically induced proximity, which uses small molecules to bring proteins together and change how they function. Related approaches include PROTACs, which trigger the breakdown of specific proteins, and transcriptional/epigenetic chemically induced proximity (TCIP), which alters gene regulation.

In a recent development, “Our molecules consist of two inhibitors joined by a carefully designed short linker. By gluing two cancer-driving proteins together, they alter the proteins’ natural interactions,” said senior study author Shaomeng Wang, PhD, Warner-Lambert/Parke-Davis Professor in Medicine, professor of internal medicine, pharmacology and medicinal chemistry, and director of the Michigan Center for Therapeutic Innovation.

Sources indicate that the team tested DALTAC molecules in prostate cancer cell lines, mouse models, and three-dimensional organoids derived from human cells. The molecules were more effective at killing tumor cells than combining separate AR and p300 inhibitors, with less toxicity to normal cells. In animal studies, they produced lasting responses and worked against tumors resistant to standard treatments.

“Our optimized molecule is approximately 1,000 times more potent in tumor cells than the combination of inhibitors targeting these proteins separately, while sparing normal cells that lack these interactions. We also optimized the molecules for oral bioavailability, a key step toward developing a pill for patients,” Wang said.

The findings, published in Nature, resulted from a collaboration between Chinnaiyan’s laboratory, which specializes in prostate cancer biology, and Wang’s laboratory, which focuses on medicinal chemistry and drug discovery.

In a recent development, “These are remarkable preclinical results,” Chinnaiyan noted. “The durable responses suggest an opportunity to develop a more effective treatment for advanced prostate cancer, including castration-resistant prostate cancer, if these findings translate to patients.”.

The research remains at the preclinical stage, and the approach has not yet been tested in humans.

“Our teams are working closely to identify a drug candidate suitable for testing in human clinical trials,” Wang said.

The researchers also believe that changing how proteins interact could offer a broader strategy for developing treatments against other cancers and protein targets beyond AR and p300.

Reference: “Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer” by Jie Luo, Jianzhang Yang, Jean Ching-Yi Tien, Mi Wang, Sumit Das, Xiaoju Wang, Eleanor Young, Jelena Tošović, Rahul Mannan, Weiguo Xiang, Xia Jiang, Jocelyn Cai, Yihan Liu, Kenneth Gu, Somnath Mahapatra, Shiting Li, Yitong Yin, Sanjana Eyunni, Abigail J. Todd, Shicheng Jin, Xuhong Cao, Fengyun Su, Stephanie J. Miner, Ranga Sudharshan, Arvind Rao, Abhijit Parolia, Yuanyuan Qiao, Shaomeng Wang and Arul M. Chinnaiyan, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11262-4.

This work was supported by the Rogel Cancer Center Proteomics Resource Facility Shared Resource.

Disclosure: Wang and Chinnaiyan are cofounders of and hold equity in Medsyn Biopharma. The University of Michigan has filed patents related to the AR-p300 DALTACs, which have been licensed to Medsyn. U-M has received a research contract from Medsyn, for which Wang serves as the principal investigator.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sitting here on the outskirts of our Milky Way Galaxy, itâs hard to imagine the galactic machinations that led to our goldilocks spot around a very welcoming yellow dwarf star.
  • As observations by NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) now reveal, massive galaxies have largescale gaseous outflows that greatly quench their star production.
  • And as the authors of a newly introduced paper in the journal Astrophysics and Space Science describe, JWST has observed a link between outflows from a massive galaxyâs central core and the quenching of star formation at so-called âCosmic Noon.â That is, roughly 8-12 billion years ago, when the number of stars forming per unit volume in the cosmos reached its peak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sitting here on the outskirts of our Milky Way Galaxy, itâs hard to imagine the galactic machinations that led to our goldilocks spot around a very welcoming yellow dwarf star. But for decades, astronomers have suspected that the internal dynamics of massive galaxies like ours play an outsized role in regulating star formation.

As observations by NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) now reveal, massive galaxies have largescale gaseous outflows that greatly quench their star production.

And as the authors of a newly introduced paper in the journal Astrophysics and Space Science describe, JWST has observed a link between outflows from a massive galaxyâs central core and the quenching of star formation at so-called âCosmic Noon.â That is, roughly 8-12 billion years ago, when the number of stars forming per unit volume in the cosmos reached its peak.

Outflows are large-scale flows of gas, from inside to outside the galaxy usually caused by either supernovae or energetic outbursts from supermassive black holes.

These JWST observations have revealed that outflows are more abundant and more powerful than we thought, suggesting that the evolution of galaxies is strongly impacted by outflows, Sirio Belli, an associate professor at the University of Bologna, Italy and the paperâs co-author, told me via email.

Normally, galaxies are rich in gas, and when the gas is sufficiently cold, it collapses under its own weight and forms a dense cloud from which newly introduced stars form. But such outflows likely remove a large quantity of gas from galaxies, which are then unable to form new stars.

Growing supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies drive powerful winds, blowing away gas that would otherwise form stars, Rebecca Davies, the paperâs lead author and an astrophysicist at Australiaâs Swinburne University of Technology in Melbourne, told me via email. With JWST, we can measure the amount of cold star-forming gas being ejected, Davies told me.

But JWST has also revealed that outflows powered by accretion onto supermassive black holes are linked to the rapid shut-down or âquenchingâ of star formation.

As for what leads to such quenching?

Quenching can happen if the galaxy runs out of gas or the galaxy stops being able to turn the gas into stars because the gas is too hot or turbulent to collapse, claims Davies.

One possibility is that the supermassive black hole at the center of the galaxy releases a large amount of energy which removes and/or heats the gas and prevents the formation of fresh stars, says Belli.

As such massive galaxies age, their AGN become relatively quiescent, not unlike Sag A* --- our own Milky Wayâs supermassive black hole in our galactic center.

The Milky Wayâs black hole had a major flare just a few million years ago, smaller outbursts only a century or two ago, and it still flickers almost every day as hot gas swirls just outside it, says Davies.

A key open question is what triggers outflows powerful enough to quench galaxies.

Sources indicate that outflows are very common in massive galaxies at cosmic noon, but most of these galaxies are not quenching: the outflows simply keep the galaxies in equilibrium and prevent them from converting all their gas into stars too quickly, says Davies. Possible triggers of the most powerful outflows include galaxy mergers, or radio jets launched by the central supermassive black holes, she says.

As for how this stellar quenching might impact the formation of molecular clouds that spawn solar type stars and habitable planetary systems?

When galaxies are quenched, the formation of new stars and planets is shut down, with strong repercussions on the probability of developing habitable systems, states Belli. If the Milky Way had been quenched at Cosmic Noon, it would likely not have formed many new stars in the last 10 billion years, and our solar system which is only 5 billion years old would not exist today, he says.

But star formation can become too much of a good thing.

When star formation is too strong there are other problems, such as the large number of stellar explosions that could negatively impact the habitability of planets, claims Belli. The connection between galaxy-scale processes and the habitability of planetary systems is only now being investigated, he says.

ZWO Seestar S30 Plus review

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2207 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus.
  • Editing controls could be a little more responsive.
  • Sources indicate that why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus. The image quality is great, it's easy to use, and it's compact and lightweight enough to take it anywhere. It's not quite as good as the more expensive S30 Pro, but it's a nice middle-ground option between the S30 and the S30 Pro that gives you a lot of features for the money.

Seestar app is reliable and easy to navigate.

All-in-one workflow from shooting to sharing.

2K image quality is better than we expected.

Lightweight and easy to travel with.

Editing controls could be a little more responsive.

Not suitable for smaller planetary nebulas.

Sources indicate that why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you. Find out more about how we test.

ZWO has just released the newest member of its smart telescope range: the Seestar S30 Plus. This all-in-one smart telescope is designed for beginners and hobbyists who want an affordable way into astrophotography that won't leave you scratching your head, and lets you capture, process and share your images in one simple workflow. It sits between the Seestar S30 and S30 Pro, and is priced at $499 for its release.

With 2K image quality, a light pollution filter and a user-friendly interface, it's a smart telescope that anyone can enjoy, regardless of your experience level, and regardless of whether you're shooting from your city balcony or a dark sky site. Like the other models, it uses dual cameras to capture a wide range of subjects, including deep-sky objects with the telephoto camera, and constellations, star trails and the Milky Way with the wide-angle camera. It's lightweight and easy to travel with, and it even comes with a separate solar filter for solar imaging and eclipse time-lapses.

We got our hands on an advance copy to test ahead of its release, so we put it through its paces on several different celestial subjects.

Industry observers note that the Seestar S30 Plus is one of the smallest, most compact smart telescopes on the market, weighing just 3.63 pounds (1.65 kg) and measuring 8.3 x 5.5 x 3.2 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm). Its sleek, matte white design looks identical to the other Seestar models (we compared it to our S30 Pro), except for the branding on the unit itself.

In a recent development, it comes in a padded soft carry case and includes a small tripod (although we always prefer to use our own), a solar filter, a 40-inch (1 meter) USB-A to USB-C charging cable, a removable shoulder strap for the carry case, and a quick-start guide. With its accessories and case, the whole setup weighs 4.89 pounds (2.22 kg).

On the unit itself, you'll find just one button, which powers it on, plus the USB-C port on the side. Super simple, although we'd have liked the USB-C port to be covered to prevent moisture or dust from getting in.

Recent findings suggest that the set-up process couldn't be easier. When you turn the telescope on, you'll hear a double beep and see the power button light up alongside the red dots on the black screen to indicate the battery level. Four dots mean the battery is full. The telescope will tell you when it's ready to connect, at which point you can sync it up to the app on your smartphone or tablet. To turn it off, you just select "Shutdown" in the app, which closes the arm and turns the unit off.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It also features an anti-dew heater, which we've found works quite well in mild to moderate humidity. On a couple of our shoots, we noticed a tiny bit of condensation forming on the unit when the humidity was higher, so we wouldn't feel confident leaving it unsupervised for long periods on a particularly dewy evening. (We used the Clear Outside app to monitor the humidity levels.).

Sources indicate that the Seestar App is user-friendly and easy to navigate, with just the right amount of controls: you have plenty of options to choose from but it doesn’t become overwhelming. The main Seestar page is where you'll likely spend most of your time, as this is where you can search for celestial objects to shoot, access your album, initiative a shoot and read up on what objects Seestar recommends based on your time and location.

Recent findings suggest that the Stargazing section is where you can select or search for the subject you want to shoot. You can use the search function to find a specific target or browse Tonight's Best, and you can also search through different types of subjects like galaxies, nebulas, clusters and more. From here, you can also select planets, track comets and photograph constellations using the wide camera.

Click on a subject and the app will display information about it, including its current altitude and coordinates, which help determine what time is best to shoot that particular object. It automatically applies the appropriate filters and settings, but you can override these if you want to.

There's very little to complain about when it comes to using the app. It has lots of information for beginners, so you don't need a ton of knowledge about the night sky, and everything is fairly self-explanatory. There were a couple of occasions when it failed to calibrate itself (for example, when we tried to locate the Pleiades, which had just risen above a tree), and other times when we chose a new target and it slewed the long way round instead of only having to move slightly. But otherwise, the app worked well.

Industry observers note that the AI Enhance section has some good editing tools to bring out the best from your photos. You can reduce the stars, adjust the brightness, contrast, saturation and RGB curves, apply denoise and eliminate any satellite trails — although we'd love a dehaze slider to bring out some of the fainter nebulosity of certain objects. The sliders could do with being a little more responsive, especially the RGB curves, but overall, it does a pretty good job of editing your pictures to get a pleasing result.

In a recent development, we had about 10 days to test our review unit before its release on November 10, so we could only capture as much as the weather permitted in that time. All our tests were conducted from our backyard in a Bortle 4 region, and captured before moonrise to eliminate as much light pollution as possible. Due to these time constraints, we aimed to capture our images for a total of 60 minutes each, although we'd ideally have aimed for longer in some cases.

In a recent development, nov. 16, 2026: Lunar, solar and Heart Nebula images and information added.

In a recent development, now for the fun part — the images. The Seestar S30 Plus has a focal length of 160mm, which is advantageous for capturing large subjects like the Andromeda Galaxy, the North America Nebula and the Pleiades. Large emission nebulas are where it really shines; however, the focal length is too short to capture smaller apparent objects.

For this review, we aimed to capture as many different types of objects as possible. All our images were edited in the Seestar app with, in some cases, a few minor tweaks in Lightroom. You also have the option to download the individual files to your computer to process them yourself in dedicated astrophotography software, which is advantageous if you're a more experienced user.

Recent findings suggest that everyone's favorite star cluster, the Pleiades, was one of the first targets we wanted to capture. We could see the faint blue nebulosity after as little as 15 minutes of integration time, and it only improved over time. After 60 minutes, we had a really nice image and could easily bring out the blue haze via the editing tools in the app. However, we got a much more impressive result after tweaking our image a little further in Lightroom, bringing out even more haze and reflective dust.

It has been revealed that the Andromeda Galaxy is a perfect target for the Seestar S30 Plus. It takes up a large portion of the frame, and with long integration times, it can reveal beautiful details in the faint outer arms. We shot for around an hour in our tests due to weather and time constraints, but we still got an impressive image. As we approached 60 minutes, there was a lot of cloud cover, and we noticed it struggling to stack images toward the end of the session, so we stopped the integration at 57 minutes.

Andromeda is certainly going to be the most impressive galaxy for the Seestar visually, as most others will appear smaller in the frame and will need longer integration, so make sure you have a clear, dark night for it.

Large emission nebulas are where the Seestar S30 Plus thrives, and the North America Nebula is a great target. It covers the whole field of view, and the red hydrogen gas easily comes to the forefront of the image.

It has been revealed that the Eastern Veil Nebula and Heart Nebula are also lovely targets for the Seestar S30 Plus. In the Eastern Veil Nebula in particular, you can bring out the beautiful red and turquoise hues in as little as 15 minutes, but longer integration times will yield brighter, more colorful results.

Recent findings suggest that planetary nebulas are where you will see the limitations of the Seestar's 160mm focal length. Most planetary nebulas have a very small apparent size — we've previously captured the Dumbbell Nebula and Cocoon Nebula with our S30 Pro, and they were a tiny dot in the middle of the screen. We tried the Helix Nebula, and even though it's one of the largest apparent planetary nebulas, it's still fairly small on the Seestar S30 Plus. You can still get a decent image of it, but if you want to focus on imaging planetary nebulas, you'll need a bigger scope. Because it was very low in the sky and there was some interfering cloud, we stopped integration at 27 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that solar and lunar imaging is easier than ever thanks to the Seestar S30 Plus. The included solar filter is easy to attach to the front of the telescope (and should be used for every solar session). Solar mode is ideal for viewing sunspots and creating a timelapse of a solar eclipse — we captured the total solar eclipse with our S30 Pro back in the summer. Similarly, lunar imaging gives you the option to capture images, video and timelapses of the moon, and we were impressed with the detail we got on a crescent moon, particularly at 2x. On both solar and lunar modes, you can shoot at 1x, 2x and 4x.

The Seestar S30 Plus is an affordable entry point into deep-sky astrophotography without the confusing settings and expensive setup. It's ideal for beginners, although more experienced users will likely want to upgrade to the superior image quality and extra features of the S30 Pro.

Sources indicate that still, for under $500, we can't complain. Not only is the Seestar S30 Plus easy to navigate and use, but it teaches you about space in a fun and interactive way, and you don't need to spend hours stacking individual frames on your computer to process — although you still can do that if you want more control over your editing.

If you want better image quality.

It has been revealed that if you can stretch your budget, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade. It produces 4K images and offers more pro-level features.

Read our full Seestar S30 Pro review.

If you want a longer focal length.

To see deeper into space, the Seestar S50 Pro has a longer focal length of 260mm and a larger 50mm aperture, making it better for smaller apparent objects.

Read our full Seestar S50 Pro review.

If you want a more traditional telescope.

If the imaging aspect doesn't interest you, the Celestron StarSense Explorer range of telescopes connects to your phone to guide you around the sky, but you observe the cosmos through an eyepiece instead of capturing it on your phone.

Read our full Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ review.

In a recent development, kimberley Lane, E-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, reviewing camera gear from Sony, Canon, OM System and more. With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.

Don’t let cocktails fall by the wayside in the flurry of holiday dinner prep — these drinks make the party.

In the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic, totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch.

It has been revealed that now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Below, find Eater editor-approved recipes for cocktails that will add the most festive of feelings to every holiday gathering.

It has been revealed that I host a holiday potluck with a core group of friends in December, and one of my favorite potential additions is whatever punch that drinks columnist M. Carrie Allan is cooking up over at the Washington Post. A favorite from 2022 was a meringue-topped citrus punch, featuring blood orange, Aperol, and a dramatic meringue topping. Noted topping adds undeniable flair and drama to the presentation, but if you’re daunted by the idea, the punch itself is still a festive, not-too-sweet drink to serve, celebrating winter citrus. —Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

It has been revealed that meaghan Dorman’s modern classic is a favorite year-round, but there’s something about the holidays that calls for Scotch. No shade to the nog freaks, but the subtly spiced sour is a pleasant counterpoint to the onslaught of holiday food and beverage maximalism. No need to break out the single malt either, your dusty bottle of Dewars or Monkey Shoulder will do just fine. —Allison Hamlin, director of network development.

It has been revealed that the French 75 — the effervescent classic cocktail made with gin, Champagne, and lemon — is already one of my easy-drinking favorites, and I like it even better in punch form, accented with an aesthetically pleasing ice block of cheery lemon slices. What makes it 77 instead of 75? The substitution of St-Germain (or any elderflower liqueur) for simple syrup, adding just a tiny touch of herbal complexity. It’s perfect for Fresh Year’s Eve, but just as refreshing at Thanksgiving or any other holiday table where you want something light and zesty. —Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

It has been revealed that as the de facto cook for Thanksgiving, I like to keep the drinks options simple so I can focus on food prep. This cocktail recipe requires only two ingredients, doesn’t require pre-batching, and is easy enough for people to pour on their own. I also like how it uses Basque cider, which is drier than the typical ciders, so it’s not too sweet while still tapping into that cozy fall feeling —Rayna Rossitto, editor, branded content.

I grew up guzzling Broguiere’s eggnog, but I love the more tropical combination of rich, creamy coconut milk, rum, and cinnamon in coquito; the Puerto Rican holiday cocktail was first described to me as “eggnog, if it went on vacation,” and I haven’t looked back since. This version is by bartender Shannon Ponche, and gets extra dressed up in spice for the holidays with the addition of a homemade cinnamon simple syrup, a woody, nutty oloroso sherry, and a splash of spiced Braulio. —Francky Knapp, staff writer.

It has been revealed that there are two schools of thought on a post-dinner drink: You could go for a bracing digestif to “aid digestion,” or you could indulge in a liquid dessert that swaddles you in sugar, fat, and everything nice. I’m notoriously bad at decision making, so I tend to split the difference with an eggy flip tinged with something bitter. Together, a whole egg and syrup (in this case honey syrup) build a comforting base, while an entire 1.5 ounces of cocktail bitters (as opposed to the usual dash or two) ensure you don’t entirely fall asleep in your glass. Angostura is a great option, delivering some classic holiday spice, but any style of cocktail bitters would probably work, as would an amaro. Dry shaking (shaking the liquid ingredients without ice) is key to achieving a frothy texture, and don’t forget the half-ounce of whiskey, which punches up the rest of the flavors. —Nick Mancall-Bitel, editor.

Several members of my husband’s family are Manhattan drinkers, so I expect that my decision to serve the Grandfather cocktail during Thanksgiving appetizers will be a hit. It’s a riff on the classic drink with a hint of fall, courtesy of the addition of Applejack, an apple brandy. It’s smooth and well-balanced. It’s also quite boozy, so I’ll probably look for a slightly lower-proof option to tide us over after that initial round. I’ve had success with a bourbon and ginger ale bar (with various sodas and mixers) in the past, as well as Smitten Kitchen’s fall sangria; maybe this year we’ll go with her (okay, still pretty boozy) apple cider Old Fashioneds. —Missy Frederick, cities director.

Scientists Discover Two Monster Black Holes at the Dawn of Time That Shouldn’t Exist

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (716 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A rare cosmic discovery offers latest clues about how early galaxy interactions may have fueled the rapid growth of supermassive black holes.
  • Astronomers have discovered two enormous black holes shining as quasars just 900 million years after the Massive Bang, challenging theories of how supermassive black holes formed in the early Universe.
  • The system, designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, is the most distant compact quasar pair ever identified.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A rare cosmic discovery offers latest clues about how early galaxy interactions may have fueled the rapid growth of supermassive black holes.

Astronomers have discovered two enormous black holes shining as quasars just 900 million years after the Massive Bang, challenging theories of how supermassive black holes formed in the early Universe. One contains roughly 1.5 billion times the Sun’s mass, while its companion weighs about 400 million solar masses.

The system, designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, is the most distant compact quasar pair ever identified. Its two members are separated by approximately 18,100 light-years, about one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way.

According to recent reports, “There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two,” says Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab who led the international study. “We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.”.

Industry observers note that quasars are intensely luminous regions surrounding actively feeding supermassive black holes. As gas spirals inward, it heats up and releases tremendous amounts of radiation, sometimes outshining every star in the surrounding galaxy.

It has been revealed that during the Universe’s first billion years, galaxies rapidly assembled within growing concentrations of dark matter. Galaxy collisions and mergers could funnel gas toward central black holes, fueling their growth. Yet the enormous masses of Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua remain difficult to explain within the limited time available.

The discovery emerged from the Aether survey, a James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) program led by Emanuele Paolo Farina of NSF NOIRLab/Gemini. Researchers examined 200 early quasars, representing approximately 43% of those known from this period, using Webb’s Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit.

While inspecting the observations, scientists noticed that quasar J1602+4228A appeared to have a faint companion. Follow-up observations with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaiʻi confirmed that the two sources could be distinguished individually, despite their exceptionally close apparent separation.

Industry observers note that “The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights,” notes Onorato. Additional observations helped researchers further characterize both quasars.

Astronomers expect pairs of active black holes to form as galaxies interact and merge. However, black holes shine as quasars for relatively short periods, making it difficult to catch two neighboring objects in this luminous phase simultaneously.

In a recent development, the challenge is even greater in the distant Universe, where faint objects separated by tiny angles are difficult to resolve. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is only the third known quasar pair discovered during cosmic dawn, when the first generations of galaxies and black holes were taking shape.

Researchers suggest that Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua may lie in an exceptionally dense region of the early Universe, where frequent galaxy interactions supplied gas for rapid star formation and black hole growth. This remains a possible explanation rather than a confirmed account of the system’s origins.

Sources indicate that “Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment,” states Onorato. “It’s a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times.”.

The Hawaiian nickname translates to “Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.” It was created through the A Hua He Inoa program in collaboration with Hawaiian language and astronomy institutions.

In a recent development, reference: “Nāpōwawā‘enakaulua: A Close Quasar Pair at Cosmic Dawn in the Aether Survey” by Silvia Onorato, Emanuele Paolo Farina, Roberto Decarli, Klaudia Protušová, Elia Pizzati, Debora Pelliccia, Devin S. #30943. China Signals Its Intention to Land on Jupiter's Moon Callisto

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1379 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Universetoday ↗ Open Full Page

China Signals Its Intention to Land on Jupiter's Moon Callisto

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1379 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The China National Space Administration (CNSA) has been talking about a mission to the Jovian system since 2018.
  • Tianwen-4 obviously isn't a sample return mission.
  • The CNSA confirmed a latest opportunity for payloads for its Tianwen-4 mission to Jupiter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The China National Space Administration (CNSA) has been talking about a mission to the Jovian system since 2018. It's named Tianwen-4, and it will build on the success of other recent missions like Chang'e 6, which collected the first sample from the lunar far side in 2024.

Tianwen-4 obviously isn't a sample return mission. But according to recent developments, it will attempt another extremely challenging mission profile: a landing on Callisto.

The CNSA confirmed a latest opportunity for payloads for its Tianwen-4 mission to Jupiter.

Industry observers note that "The primary objectives of the Tianwen-4 mission are to achieve Jovian orbiting, as well as orbiting and landing exploration of Callisto, and to advance scientific research on the Jovian system," the announcement reads. To improve the mission's performance and success, the CNSA is asking for instrument proposals from within China and from outside partners.

The orbiter itself will carry 10 instruments, and the payload will include multiple cameras, imagers, and spectrometers, as well as a particle detector and a magnetometer. But the announcement also addresses the needs of a Callisto Lander.

"The lander is planned to carry 2 scientific payloads: Callisto Surface Composition Analyzer and Callisto Lander Magnetometer," it reads.

It has been revealed that the surface composition analyzer will be a Raman spectrometer. Raman spectrometers can analyze the composition of rocks with the light from a laser, and are becoming a standard part of planetary missions. NASA's Perseverance rover uses an ultraviolet Raman spectrometer to measure fine-scale mineralogy and to detect organic matter. The ESA's upcoming Rosalind Franklin rover will have one, and JAXA's Martian Moons Explorer carries one in its IDEFIX rover.

Sources indicate that callisto's surface is heterogenous on a small scale. There are small bright patches that seem to be pure water ice and there are other patches that appear to be a mixture of rock and ice. These are intermixed with larger, darker areas that are not ice. But spectral identification is uncertain. The Tianwen-4 lander and its Raman spectrometer should be able to determine the compositions of these components. There's also lots of carbon on the surface, and the instrument should be able to tell if its primordial carbon or altered carbon.

This mosaic of Callisto images from the Voyager 1 mission demonstrates a large-scale feature named Valhalla. It's an old impact crater with concentric rings expanding outward. They extend outward for about 1,500 km, and a bright central point, probably the original impact basin, is about 600 km across. Image Credit: NASA/JPL.

In a recent development, while Jupiter's other moons like Ganymede, and especially Europa, have strong evidence for subsurface oceans, Callisto's composition and structure is less certain. It appears to be partially differentiated, and magnetometer readings are ambiguous regarding an ocean. But if the Tianwen-4 lander's Raman spectrometer can determine if some of its surface composition is aqueously altered, that would be evidence in favour of an ocean.

The lander's other instrument will be a surface magnetometer. By combining its data with the data from the orbiter's magnetometer, ionospheric signals and signals from the moon's surface can be separated. That will reveal more about its interior, especially regarding its potential subsurface ocean.

It would be nice to have a better understanding of Callisto, since it and the other Galilean moons are expected to have formed in-situ, unlike some other Solar System moons. Some of those appear to be captured objects. So understanding Callisto is an avenue to understanding Jupiter itself, the dominant planet in our system.

Callisto's internal structure is uncertain, but it seems to be differentiated, with multiple ice layers and a rock and metal core. It may also have a saltwater ocean, but is far from certain. Image Credit: By Kelvinsong - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/31643955.

Landing on any of the Galilean moons is challenging, but Callisto might be the least challenging. It's probably not the best scientific destination among them, but it is the most accessible. For one thing, it's outside Jupiter's extremely powerful radiation belts, where radiation is strong enough to degrade sensitive instruments after short exposure times. Think of NASA's Juno spacecraft and its wide orbit. It only makes short dives into the radiation belts. Even then, Juno protects its most sensitive parts inside a titanium vault.

Industry observers note that callisto is furthest from Jupiter compared to the other three Galilean moons, so its gravity well is shallower. Less precious propellant is required to land there. Tianwen-4 can also use gravity assists at Callisto to prepare for orbital insertion.

Sources indicate that callisto is further away from Jupiter than the other Galilean moons. The other three are deeper inside its magnetic fields and powerful radiation belts, which makes visiting them much more hazardous. The radiation dose on Callisto's surface is weaker and won't take such a heavy toll on sensitive electronics. Image Credit: By B. Smithin Szalay, J. R., Smith, H. T., Zirnstein, E. J., McComas, D. J., Begley, L. J., Bagenal, F., et al. (2022). Water-group pickup ions from Europa-genic neutrals orbiting Jupiter. Geophysical Research Letters, 49, e2022GL098111.

Sources indicate that another reason Callisto is the preferred moon for a surface mssion is the its surface. Callisto's surface is ancient, cratered, and stable. It's a geologically quiet place compared to Io, for instance. It doesn't suffer from the same tidal heating and constant volcanic upheaval that Io suffers from. There are no mountains or volcanoes, only ancient crater on top of ancient crater. This makes hazard avoidance easier, since orbital images are unlikely to have changed from the time they were captured to the time the lander arrives there.

But Callisto is still challenging. It's an airless moon, and that creates its own difficulties. Atmospheric breaking isn't an option. The time delay also ranges from about 35 to 50 minutes, so round-trip communication is double that. That means the landing must be autonomous.

According to recent reports, the best surface images come from the Galileo mission, and that spacecraft imaged most of Callisto at poor resolution. Only some small areas are imaged at higher resolutions of tens of meters per pixel.

Recent findings suggest that this image of Callisto is made from data from Galileo and Voyager 1 and 2. It emphasizes how heavily cratered the moon's ancient surface is, and how uniform it is. There are a few smooth areas, and no mountains of volcanoes. Image Credit: NASA/JPL/DLR.

But the mission initiative calls for Tianwen-4 to orbit Callisto at an altitude of 300 km. Galileo got to within 138 km of the moon, but that was 25 years ago. Camera technology has advanced since then, and Tianwen-4 will carry a pair of visible light imaging cameras. One of them, the wide-angle camera (JWAC), is dedicated to mapping Callisto's surface and topography. Tianwen-4's proposed mapping orbit is 300 km in altitude. From that height, the JWAC operates at about 90 meters per pixel.

Sources indicate that in 2020, the CNSA outlined a timeline for the Tianwen-4 mission that would see it launch in September of 2029. To preserve precious propellant, the spacecraft will perform a slingshot flyby of Venus in April 2030, then a pair of slingshots with Earth in 2031 and 2033.

Sources indicate that in 2035 it will reach Jupiter and enter an orbit around the gas giant, also making flybys of irregular moons. That's phase one. Phase two starts with two gravity assists with Callisto, then in February 2038, it will enter an orbit around the moon. At some point after that, the Callisto lander will be released.

This strategy was first outlined in 2020, so it will likely be changed. The instrumentation on the orbiter could be changed, too, and that includes its mapping camera and its resolution. But with their call for instrument proposals, the CNSA is making one thing clear: they intend to land on Callisto.

Whether you’re a fan of savory dishes, prefer fruit pies, or love the wobble of a perfectly set custard pie, there is a pie for everyone — including Eater staffers.

In a recent development, we love a super-easy no-bake pie just as much as we love a more complex, picture-perfect creation. Here are some of our favorite pie recipes to make at home this holiday season and beyond.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

It has been revealed that since I grew up in Los Angeles and had never heard of buttermilk pie, it may come as a surprise that it’s one of my go-to pies to make. I discovered it seven years ago on a Twitter thread about unique, regional pies and was fascinated enough by this classic Southern dessert to attempt it, trying the first recipe that came up on my Google search. This is that recipe, and it has been consistently easy and perfect since that very first pie I made. The filling is smooth and velvety with subtle notes of nutmeg and a kiss of lemon. It reminds me of dan tat, or Chinese egg tarts, but it’s way less fussy. Yes, you can make your own pie crust, but storebought works well here, too, because the real star is the wobbly buttermilk custard. — Kat Thompson, audience editor.

Industry observers note that when fall comes around, I turn to this tried and true caramelized onion and butternut squash tart from Food 52 over and over again. It’s a perfect savory option to bring to Friendsgiving, Thanksgiving, or any autumnal get together. What I love most about it is that it highlights flavors and ingredients of the season while standing out from the plentiful pumpkin and pecan pies that you’re sure to find at any gathering. To make it heartier, I sometimes add crumbled sausage to the mix. — Terri Ciccone, deputy director of audience development.

The only thing my mom and I love more than re-invigorating this incredibly simple chess pie recipe is telling the (most likely made up) story behind the name. Trying on my grandmother’s Texas twang, we explain how a server at a diner was once asked the flavor of the custard pie that day. She said, “It’s just pie,” but with her Southern accent that was mistaken as “chess pie.” And so we got this simple custard pie, which is filled with evaporated milk and set perfectly with cornmeal. My mom started experimenting with adding edible lavender oil to the recipe, which has became my favorite way to bake it, but she’s also added a tablespoon or two of my dad’s “Mexican mocha” (spiced hot chocolate) mix to make an incredible chocolate custard pie with a kick. But even plain, this pie recipe is always a substantial hit. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

I have nothing but the utmost respect for people who lovingly make intricately crafted, high-maintenance pies with lattice crusts and the whole shebang, but my personal tried-and-true, always-go-back pie recipe is one I’ve frequently revisited since high school: no-bake chocolate peanut butter pie. I do not know the true origin of the semi-homemade, Sandra Lee-esque creation, but if you stumble upon some version of the five-ish-ingredient recipe that includes Cool Whip, like this one on the blog Crazy for Crust, that’s what I’m referring to. Rest assured that I generally have the taste and standards of a bougie person, but this extremely simple, absolutely-not-healthy recipe is just perfection. It’s sweet, salty, creamy, and simultaneously light, fluffy, rich, and decadent. Whenever I make it for a dinner party, holiday gathering, or potluck, it garners rave reviews (the word “orgasmic” has been used to describe it more than once). And as a child of the ‘90s, I love using an Oreo crust and Skippy peanut butter — forever crowd-pleasers. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Recent findings suggest that “We have Milk Bar at home, honey” is what comes to mind whenever I make this pie, which reminds me of the New York City bakery’s famous, albeit once salaciously named dessert (now called the Milk Bar Pie). This butterscotch pie from Smitten Kitchen packs the same gooey, buttery taste and a satisfyingly sticky consistency — I feel like it’s a pie for people who wish they could just eat caramelized graham cracker crusts and custards for dessert. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Anna Theoktisto, Southern Living.

It has been revealed that this zingy citrus pie might evoke summertime, but that’s exactly why I make sure it’s on the table during the holidays. Somewhere between a lemon pie and an icebox pudding, Atlantic Beach Pie delivers the bracing acidity I crave after a marathon of rich food. It originated at a North Carolina seafood restaurant, acting as a clever loophole to the old wives’ tale that eating dessert after a seafood meal could be deadly. Believe the lore or not, this pie is bound to earn seconds, whether for its salty, buttery saltine crust, zippy custard filling, or cloud of velvety whipped cream. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Claudia Fleming, adapted by Amanda Hesser for the Upcoming York Times.

Industry observers note that I am not a pie person, per se — I hate the pressure of making a flaky crust — but I don’t mind the less-stress approach of making a tart, which asks only that I press dough into a tart pan. This famous chocolate caramel tart, a version of which my mom made frequently when I was growing up, is a dish I would definitely have on my roster if Mythical Kitchen ever invited me onto Last Meals. With dark chocolate ganache, a caramel filling that’s made more complex by the addition of salt and creme fraiche, and a sprinkling of a little more flaky salt on top, it tastes like a slightly more sophisticated Twix Bar.

I once asked my mom to make it for an ex-boyfriend, with me talking it up to him as my favorite dessert ever, and when he told me it was “just okay” — and who says that, especially when presented with a free dessert that required the dessert-giver to make a caramel? — that was the final sign I needed that he was not the one for me. Lesson learned: My husband and I are very dessert-compatible. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Josh Walker & Duolan Li, Bon Appétit.

Breaking: Scientists Discover a Bizarre Quantum State That Exists at Room Temperature

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With each laser pulse, a room-temperature supersolid selects a new arrangement, revealing how crystal-like order can emerge without being locked to one position.
  • Recent findings suggest that studying unusual quantum states often requires expensive equipment that cools samples almost to absolute zero.
  • Recent findings suggest that A superfluid has no viscosity, the internal resistance that opposes flow in an ordinary fluid, so it can pass through extremely narrow channels without resistance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With each laser pulse, a room-temperature supersolid selects a new arrangement, revealing how crystal-like order can emerge without being locked to one position.

Recent findings suggest that studying unusual quantum states often requires expensive equipment that cools samples almost to absolute zero. Researchers have now observed a supersolid at room temperature, using a system that strongly links light and matter. This unusual state combines the repeating pattern of a crystal with the frictionless flow of a superfluid.

Recent findings suggest that A superfluid has no viscosity, the internal resistance that opposes flow in an ordinary fluid, so it can pass through extremely narrow channels without resistance. If you moved an oar through one, you would feel almost no drag until you exceeded a critical speed, when swirling quantum vortices would appear. A supersolid retains this fluid behavior while developing crystal-like order.

The TopoLight consortium’s study, published in Science Advances, involved researchers from the Faculty of Physics at the University of Warsaw, the Military University of Technology in Poland, IBM Research Zurich, and the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS).

According to recent reports, the team built its system around an optical microcavity, a tiny structure that confines light. It contained a specially designed liquid crystal and a coating of organic semiconductor, a combination that allowed light and matter to interact strongly at room temperature. The most important measurements took place at IBM Research Zurich, where researchers deposited thin semiconductor films onto photonic structures fabricated at the Military University of Technology.

“We have studied the organic semiconductor MeLPPP (methyl-substituted ladder-type poly(paraphenylene) for many years and previously observed Bose-Einstein condensation in this material,” notes Thilo Stöferle from IBM Research. “This was the first time we combined it with a liquid-crystal microcavity.”.

Inside the cavity, light and electronic excitations in the material become strongly coupled, behaving as hybrid entities called exciton polaritons. These quasiparticles last only a few picoseconds, with each picosecond equal to one trillionth of a second. Even that brief lifetime is enough for them to form a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which many particles share a quantum state and behave as a coordinated whole. Such a condensate can act as a quantum superfluid.

Building the sample also started a countdown. The organic semiconductor gradually reacted with the liquid crystal, leaving the researchers only a few hours after assembly to complete all their measurements.

“We had to blueprint the entire sequence of experiments in advance,” recalls Dr. Marcin Muszyński, the paper’s first author, now a postdoctoral researcher at The City College of New York. “Repeating a measurement meant fabricating an entirely new sample.”.

Recent findings suggest that the transition to a supersolid highlighted up as regularly spaced bright fringes in the emitted light. These stripes revealed that the condensate’s density had spontaneously developed a repeating pattern, a hallmark of crystal-like order.

The stripes appeared in a different position with every laser pulse used to excite the sample. Each time, the system selected one of several equally possible arrangements, rather than reproducing a pattern fixed in place.

Sources indicate that “This is a textbook example of spontaneous symmetry breaking,” explains Professor Guillaume Malpuech from Institut Pascal (CNRS). “Theory predicted that the supersolid could choose among several equivalent states, and that is exactly what we observed.”.

Industry observers note that the emitted light also displayed a persistent spin helix, a repeating pattern in its polarization, which describes the orientation of the light’s oscillations. The condensate therefore showed two distinct forms of order at once, one in light intensity and another in polarization.

Physicists predicted supersolids as early as the 1960s, but experimental observations took more than half a century to arrive. In 2017, researchers observed supersolidity in ultracold atomic Bose-Einstein condensates. The fresh work shows that similar quantum phenomena can be explored in photonic systems operating at room temperature.

In a recent development, “Our liquid-crystal microcavities can operate even at temperatures approaching 60°C,” states Professor Wiktor Piecek from the Military University of Technology, whose group developed the liquid-crystal structures. That is about 140°F.

Recent findings suggest that the microcavities also provide the first electrically tunable platform for investigating supersolid exciton-polariton condensates. Applying an external voltage lets researchers dynamically change their optical properties, providing a flexible way to explore quantum phases of light and matter.

That control could help researchers develop practical quantum devices based on light. Potential applications include ultrafast photonic devices, neuromorphic computing accelerators that take inspiration from the brain, and highly sensitive optical sensors that exploit the supersolid phase’s exceptional sensitivity to polarization.

Reference: “Observation of a supersolid phase in a spin-orbit coupled exciton-polariton Bose-Einstein condensate” by Marcin Muszyński, Pavel Kokhanchik, Rafał Mirek, Darius Urbonas, Pietro Tassan, Piotr Kapuściński, Przemysław Oliwa, Ioannis Georgakilas, Thilo Stöferle, Rainer F. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aee4875.

Breaking: Did The First Quarks and Gluons Experience Brownian Motion? Sometimes.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there are two ways to study the earliest moments of the Universe.
  • The fluid is known as a quark-gluon plasma, which was the first matter of the cosmos.
  • Industry observers note that particle fluids generally follow Brownian motion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there are two ways to study the earliest moments of the Universe. One is to peer into the deepest, darkest regions of space. The other is to study the most dense energetic fluid we can create in particle accelerators. A new study looks at how this fluid can behave.

The fluid is known as a quark-gluon plasma, which was the first matter of the cosmos. In those earliest moments quarks churned among the sea of strong-force carrier particles, similar to the way dust particles dance in a swirl of atomosphere molecules. Only after the Universe expanded a bit did this fluid solidify into the nuclei we see today. By slamming particles together at near light speeds, we can recreate a bit of that early plasma fluid, but only for the briefest moments of time. So we study the fluid primarily by the particles generated by these collisions. In this latest study the team simulated how the fluid behaves when a heavy particle passes through it. In the lab this can be done by slamming a proton into a heavy nucleus.

Industry observers note that particle fluids generally follow Brownian motion. First observed by Robert Brown as the jiggly motion of pollen in water, it occurs when smaller particles collide with a larger particle over time. The barrage of kicks nudges the larger particle around a jiggly random path. The smaller particles also collide with each other in a similar way. On a large scale this creates many of the features of thermodynamics, such as the flow of heat and the ideal gas relation of temperature and pressure.

Sources indicate that one of the features of Brownian motion is that the distribution of particle speeds is Gaussian. Most of the particles have speeds close to the average, but there are some particles that are much faster and some that are much slower. The distribution is symmetrical; for every 10 particles moving twice as fast as the average, there should be about 10 moving half as fast. This makes sense because collisions are random.

How the Gaussian particle distribution is shifted for higher-energy collisions. Credit: Du Plessis et al.

Recent findings suggest that although a dense plasma of charged gluons is very different from a drop of water molecules, they both follow this Gaussian distribution. After all, they are both a sea of randomly colliding molecules. You would expect then that when heavy particles move through the plasma, the result would be Gaussian. All the heavy particles would be slowed down passing through the plasma, but some would slow a bit more and others a bit less because of the random collisions. This new study found that for heavy quarks in a quark-gluon plasma this is only partially true.

According to recent reports, at slower speeds the result is precisely what we would expect. Collisions are random, and heavy quarks would have a Gaussian speed distribution. But if the heavy quarks are moving at near-light speed, such as a proton in a particle collider, then the distribution is biased. The quark is much more likely to be kicked in a way that slows it down and much less likely to get a kick that speeds it up. This skews the distribution away from Gaussian.

It has been revealed that this means that when we study quark-gluon plasmas in a particle accelerator, we must take this bias into account. Using this result, we can better understand the fluid as a whole, and this could help us understand the connection between the hot dense state of the Substantial Bang and the Universe we see today.

Du Plessis, Jean F., and Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld. "Heavy Quark Transport Is Non-Gaussian beyond Leading Logarithm." Physical Review Letters 137.19 (2026): 192302. ↩.

Industry News: Quantum Breakthrough: Scientists Develop a Detector That Can Count Over 9,000 Photons

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming detector can measure hundreds of photons with less than a single photon’s uncertainty, offering scientists a sharper way to investigate quantum light and advance future technologies.
  • Scientists developing powerful quantum computers and highly sensitive cameras need ways to count individual particles of light, even when thousands arrive together.
  • It has been revealed that “Precisely counting photons becomes more challenging as their numbers increase,” said Timon Schapeler from Paderborn University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming detector can measure hundreds of photons with less than a single photon’s uncertainty, offering scientists a sharper way to investigate quantum light and advance future technologies.

Scientists developing powerful quantum computers and highly sensitive cameras need ways to count individual particles of light, even when thousands arrive together. Researchers at Paderborn University in Germany have developed a detection system capable of counting from zero to more than 9,000 photons, opening new possibilities for studying quantum light and making precise optical measurements.

It has been revealed that “Precisely counting photons becomes more challenging as their numbers increase,” said Timon Schapeler from Paderborn University. “Our approach extends photon counting to larger numbers of photons, bridging the gap between single-photon measurements and high-sensitivity optical power meters.”.

Recent findings suggest that conventional detectors struggle with this task. Devices such as avalanche photodiodes typically register whether light is present without revealing how many photons arrived. Detectors designed for larger amounts of light face another problem because electrical noise makes individual photons difficult to distinguish. To overcome these limitations, the researchers combined superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs), known for their efficiency, precise timing, and low noise, with a technique called multiplexing.

“We wanted to know how high we can push the number of photons that can be counted with SNSPDs,” mentioned Schapeler. “This led to a detector system that uses multiplexing and the intrinsic photon-number resolution of SNSPDs. Although these technologies have been individually studied, there has not previously been a demonstration of using both approaches together at this scale, which is an order of magnitude larger than previous multiplexed single-photon counting systems.”.

In a recent development, previous research had shown that SNSPDs could distinguish limited numbers of photons using precise timing measurements. To expand that capability, the team divided a single light pulse into 128 smaller pulses separated in time, then distributed them across eight detectors to create 1,024 detection bins. This arrangement spreads the incoming photons across smaller measurements while retaining information about how many photons each bin receives.

Industry observers note that “Our approach uses low-loss optical components to distribute light evenly across 1,024 detection bins while preserving photon-number information in each bin,” mentioned Tim Bartley from Paderborn University. “This enables precise measurements, while multiplexing expands the range of photon numbers the system can measure.”.

The researchers also used a detector model previously developed with Mariia Sidorova from PTB in Germany to characterize each detection bin and improve measurement accuracy. Testing laser pulses averaging between 1 and 15,000 photons, they demonstrated precise counts of up to 276 photons with uncertainty below a single photon. Achieving comparable precision with a conventional multiplexed system would require approximately 37,000 detector elements, compared with their 1,024 detection bins.

The findings, published in Optica, Optica Publishing Group’s journal for high-impact research, could help scientists develop larger quantum systems that use light to process information.

According to recent reports, “Large-scale measurement of individual photons is a cornerstone of photonic quantum computing and single-photon-level imaging,” mentioned Bartley. “With this new macroscopic photon-counting technology, we can learn a lot about how photonic quantum computers and single-photon-sensitive cameras can be scaled.”.

Although the system has only been tested with laser pulses, the researchers plan to apply it to bright quantum states of light to investigate quantum effects at larger scales. Continued improvements in SNSPD technology could also support more precise and highly sensitive measurements across a range of sensing applications.

According to recent reports, reference: “Macroscopic photon counting beating the Poisson noise limit” by 19 November 2026, Optica. DOI: 10.1364/OPTICA.604389.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.
  • Industry observers note that the sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument.
  • While we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever new ideas have been simmering since last year’s substantial meal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.

Industry observers note that the sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

While we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever new ideas have been simmering since last year’s substantial meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

According to recent reports, stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Industry observers note that every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Sources indicate that why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

In a recent development, I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

Tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

Sources indicate that this is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Sources indicate that I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

Sources indicate that if I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated quickly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be stated is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.
