Democrats flip the Senate with stunning victories in deep-red terrain

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Democrats won control of the Senate on Tuesday, sending shock waves through Washington on a historic night that saw them flip seats in deep-red states such as Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.
  • According to recent reports, hours after The Associated Press called the Senate for Democrats, the party was projected to flip the House as well.
  • Winning the Senate was considered an unlikely prospect for Democrats at the beginning of the year, given the number of red states they needed to compete in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Democrats won control of the Senate on Tuesday, sending shock waves through Washington on a historic night that saw them flip seats in deep-red states such as Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.

According to recent reports, hours after The Associated Press called the Senate for Democrats, the party was projected to flip the House as well. As of 1:50 a.m. Wednesday, Senate Democrats had wrested seven seats from Republicans — a stunning result that gives the party newly introduced powers to confront President Donald Trump in his final two years in office.

Winning the Senate was considered an unlikely prospect for Democrats at the beginning of the year, given the number of red states they needed to compete in. But strong candidate recruitment and a favorable political environment put the chamber within Democrats' grasp.

With their majority, Democrats are expected to serve as a significant check on Trump, who could now have a more difficult time advancing his nominees through the chamber.

“Against all odds, we Democrats have won the Senate, and we have five words for the American people: Relief is on the way,” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said Thursday night in Washington.

“The American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks,” the New York Democrat added. “As a result, there is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America now and on into the future.”.

The Democratic path to the majority ran through several deep-red states that have proved hostile to the party in recent years and that Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

Industry observers note that in Texas, state Rep. James Talarico defeated scandal-plagued Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the Lone Star State since 1988. Paxton had defeated Republican incumbent John Cornyn in a primary runoff earlier this year.

Sources indicate that in perhaps the biggest shocker of the night, South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews defeated appointed Sen. Darline Graham, a shocking flip in a state that last elected a Democratic senator in 1998. Graham was appointed to the Senate in July after the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, and ran for the full term with Trump’s strong endorsement.

And the longest Senate drought in the country ended Tuesday when Democrat Adam Hamilton, pastor of the nation’s largest United Methodist church, unseated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, a state that had not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years.

Other flips came in onetime battleground states that had turned decidedly red in recent cycles. In Ohio, Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown defeated Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to the Senate to complete the unfinished term of Vice President JD Vance. And in Iowa, Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson to succeed retiring GOP Sen. Joni Ernst.

In blue-leaning Maine, a 30-year Senate career came to a close with Republican Sen. Susan Collins losing her bid for a sixth term to Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson.

The night began strongly for the party, with key holds in Georgia, where Sen. Jon Ossoff easily dispatched GOP Rep. Mike Collins, and New Hampshire, where Rep. Chris Pappas defeated a comeback bid by former Sen. John E. Sununu.

Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper also gave Democrats their first flip of the night, defeating Republican Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman.

In a recent development, democrats also held the open seat in Minnesota, with Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan prevailing over former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya.

A Democratic majority in the Senate could run into a president who has noted he would become “Mr. Veto” against any legislation coming out of chambers controlled by the opposition party.

With Trump in that position, Democrats will likely push “for legislation that may set the agenda for the future in case a Democrat’s elected in 2028,” according to Christian Grose, a professor of political science and public policy at the University of Southern California.

But in a Tuesday night interview with CBS News, Trump also stated, “My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country.”.

With control of the Senate, Democrats are also poised to block Trump’s nominees, escalating the opposition they mounted while in the minority during his first two years back in office.

According to recent reports, “Very few of them are going to get through,” Schumer told Semafor in October. “It’s the quality of the candidate that matters. Thus far, Trump has a record of notoriously bad candidates.”.

Those nominees would likely extend from the Cabinet to the judicial branch, potentially even hindering confirmation of a Supreme Court pick in case of a vacancy.

Schumer told reporters ahead of the October recess: “The bottom line is, one of the reasons we want to do everything we can to take back the Senate is not let Trump put such horrible justices — MAGA justices — on the Supreme Court and the lower courts.”.

Other Democrats have agreed with that sentiment and pointed to 2016, when Mitch McConnell led the Senate and blocked the confirmation of President Barack Obama’s Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland. That left the seat open for more than a year, with Trump eventually filling the spot with Neil Gorsuch.

According to recent reports, as Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters recently: “We’ve got to do exactly what McConnell did to us.”.

Senate Democrats will also gain subpoena power, bolstering their ability to investigate Trump and his administration. Those investigations could include his handling of the conflict in Iran, his family’s business ties and wealth gains while in office, or his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

“We have a real duty to investigate all of this just absolutely blatant corruption that’s so dangerous to our national security,” Senate Judiciary member Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut noted in September, shortly after reporting emerged about wedding after-party celebrations for Trump’s eldest son, which were financed by a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin.

While Democrats in Congress could in theory pursue a third impeachment against the president, the appetite to seal the deal in the Senate would likely fall short, given they would need 67 votes to convict.

John T. Bennett contributed to this report.

Latest Update: This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.
  • Industry observers note that tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Industry observers note that tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, notes paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

Industry observers note that the bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0).

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

It has been revealed that then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

According to recent reports, blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Sources indicate that distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

Sources indicate that in a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”.

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she indicates.

It has been revealed that schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer notes. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”.

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice notes.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”.

Sources indicate that as for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”.

#30879. Trump made midterms about himself, and voters rejected him

Trump made midterms about himself, and voters rejected him

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump consistently told voters this midterm campaign to pretend he was on the ballot.
  • Voters responded by making election night a disaster for the Republican Party the president has spent a decade remaking in his own image.
  • One GOP strategist, granted anonymity to be candid, called the election results for Trump a “2006-style massacre,” referring to President George W.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump consistently told voters this midterm campaign to pretend he was on the ballot.

Voters responded by making election night a disaster for the Republican Party the president has spent a decade remaking in his own image. Trump spent his first two years back in the White House focused almost exclusively on his “Make America Great Again” base.

One GOP strategist, granted anonymity to be candid, called the election results for Trump a “2006-style massacre,” referring to President George W. Bush’s second midterms when Democrats picked up a combined 37 House and Senate seats amid frustrations with the Iraq war, the economy and other issues at home.

Industry observers note that “This is much bigger than a couple of candidates here and there. … The challenges were Americans prefer cheap gas and not the Iran conflict, and [Trump’s] tariffs were … an issue given grocery prices,” the GOP strategist said in a text message as midnight approached Tuesday in Washington, D.C. “What’s going on in Texas … could be the shot heard around the world.”.

In a recent development, that was a reference to Texas going blue on Trump’s watch, his handpicked GOP Senate nominee, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, losing his race to Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, and Trump-backed GOP Gov. Greg Abbott losing to Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa. Trump blamed Abbott, whom he had long praised, in a late-night post, calling the three-term governor a “RINO,” or Republican in name only.

Recent findings suggest that for 21 months, multiple public opinion polls charted the independent voters who pushed him to a second nonconsecutive term in 2024 steadily leaving his coalition. Many of the same polls revealed an electorate fed up with the high prices of groceries, health care, travel and other everyday items.

Sources indicate that even as voters already were casting votes Tuesday, Trump continued to dismiss the country’s “affordability” crisis, which he for months dismissed as a Democratic-manufactured lie. The president who long sold himself as the one true messenger of the forgotten American man and woman dismissed voter concerns as a “hoax.”.

Recent findings suggest that down went Senate candidates he rallied for in the homestretch of the campaign, including Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall, GOP nominees Ashley Hinson in Iowa and Michael Whatley in North Carolina, and Paxton in Texas.

Several media outlets called Democrats winning control of the House before or just after 10 p.m. Eastern time. In South Carolina, Trump backed Graham over veteran GOP Rep. Ralph Norman, and in Texas, he put his grudge against longtime Sen. John Cornyn — who didn’t endorse him to be the GOP presidential nominee in 2024 — over Paxton’s baggage.

Sources indicate that former GOP Rep. Charlie Dent stated “the president's support among Republicans has been slightly diminished leading up to this point, and I suspect it will become more diminished after the election.”.

It has been revealed that “Over the next two years, many Republicans will be looking forward, not backward, and I think that the president will be less of a factor in the party. He’ll still be a factor, don’t get me wrong, but I think less of one,” Dent stated in a telephone interview. “The [2028] presidential nominee, whoever that is, will be the one who will be trying to determine the future of the party.”.

An ever-defiant Trump took to social media Tuesday night as the results rolled in and blamed GOP candidates, writing: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Except, he had pleaded with voters for a month to “pretend” he was on the ballot.

One White House official tried to deflect blame away from the boss, writing in an email that “candidate quality matters, and President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves.”.

But Marc Short, who worked in the Trump 1.0 White House, on Tuesday night noted the blame fell squarely on 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. “It’s hard to think of a WH that’s sabotaged House and Senate candidates more than this one,” he wrote on X.

Leading up to election night, however, Trump was dug in on defending his second term’s record.

In a recent development, “The inflation is solved. … I mean, everything’s going good,” Trump mentioned Tuesday morning on “Fox & Friends” on Fox News Channel, calling his unpopular tariffs “tremendous.”.

“I mean, we have a thing going that nobody has ever seen before, and that includes China and other countries, and they will let you know,” he said.

Trump’s campaign-trail economic message was further complicated by his decision to join Israel in striking Iran. The conflict, which started Feb. 28, defied his pledge of no latest prolonged military conflicts, which had been a hallmark of his foreign policy for a decade.

Even as polls indicated majorities of Americans placing high gas and diesel prices atop their lists of most-concerning concerns, Trump for months shrugged them off, predicting oil prices would plummet, eventually.

“The onus and the blame is going to be right on the president of the United States, which of course he is going to resist,” Dent mentioned. “At his rallies, there were these never-ending comments on things that were just really not connected to what most voters care about, which was inflation and the cost of everything and how challenging their lives are, from a financial standpoint. And the president just didn’t focus on those problems and talked about all these other things that, frankly, were irrelevant.”.

Trump would not allow his party’s candidates to put distance between their campaigns and his unpopular second term.

It has been revealed that as some House and Senate GOP candidates attempted to run on messages that downplayed Trump, he unveiled the first-ever Republican midterms convention in Dallas. The primetime spectacle spanned two nights, with Trump as the headlining act on Sept. 9 and Sept. 10 at the American Airlines Center.

During his lengthy appearance on the opening night, Trump got pushback from even some Republican lawmakers when he pledged he would send every U.S. citizen $5,000 — but only if his party retained control of the House and Senate.

On night two, Trump’s loyalists in the large arena — home to the NBA’s Dallas Mavericks — agreed to his demand that they raise their right hands and declare allegiance to him.

The convention made clear Trump would not ease his grip on the GOP.

Then came his October campaign rally blitz, with the president continuing to dismiss voters' economic worries and problem cryptic threats about the accuracy of American elections and what he called Democrats' collective intention to “cheat.”.

By the end of his midterm rally sprint, Trump increasingly went for laugh lines, a striking contrast to his fire-and-brimstone events in 2016. Audiences of his supporters from Gastonia, N.C., to Corpus Christi, Texas, to Dalton, Ga., to Salina, Kan., to Wasilla, Alaska, chuckled along at times.

His closing-argument event Monday at the Reflecting Pool that sits between the Lincoln Memorial and the World War II memorial on the National Mall offered another example of Trump’s predilection for talking about matters relatively unimportant to voters. He talked about pool liners, his White House ballroom and other non-election issues.

By late Tuesday night, Trump appeared to have moved on, telling The New York Times he would accept the outcomes of the election results.

In other media interviews, the GOP president stated he was ready to meet congressional Democrats at the negotiating table but that he had his veto pen ready.

It has been revealed that “We’re going to work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for our country,” he said on a Politico livestream Tuesday. “They've already called and they want to work with me.”.

Niels Lesniewski contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

Industry observers note that A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, claims Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng notes, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

Sources indicate that we live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

It has been revealed that zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

Industry observers note that it’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

#30874. Fossils found in Thailand reveal a giant rodent that weighed about 66 pounds

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1196 w)

Fossils found in Thailand reveal a giant rodent that weighed about 66 pounds

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two fossil teeth from Thailand reveal an ancient rodent estimated to weigh 66 pounds, offering new evidence of how early rodents grew large.
  • Most rodents are small or medium-sized, but fossils reveal that some ancient species grew much larger.
  • Scientists found a fossil tooth in a coal mine in southern Thailand that belonged to an unusually large rodent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two fossil teeth from Thailand reveal an ancient rodent estimated to weigh 66 pounds, offering new evidence of how early rodents grew large.

Most rodents are small or medium-sized, but fossils reveal that some ancient species grew much larger.

Scientists found a fossil tooth in a coal mine in southern Thailand that belonged to an unusually large rodent.

The researchers believe it weighed about 30 kilograms (66 pounds). They named it Yakamys sirindhornae.

Sixty-six pounds is about what a large North American beaver weighs. Yakamys lived about 34 million years ago. The giant rodents of South America are the largest ever found but they came long after it.

The find suggests that rodents grew large earlier than fossils had shown. It also suggests they did so in more parts of the world. For now, the evidence is two teeth.

In a recent development, both teeth were found in a layer of clay inside the main coal seam of a mine in Krabi Province. They were collected by a Thai-French fossil expedition.

The project was designed by Yaowalak Chaimanee of the University of Poitiers in France.

The co-authors work in France and Canada and at Thailand’s Department of Mineral Resources. The fossils are now held by that department.

One tooth is a lower molar, which is a grinding tooth from the back of the jaw. The other is a broken piece of a lower incisor. Incisors are the long front teeth a rodent gnaws with.

The clay is roughly 35.1 million to 33.7 million years old. That age is based on other mammals found at the site and on magnetism preserved in the rock.

In the name Yakamys, the word yak is Thai for giant and mys is Greek for mouse or rat.

The species name honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn for her long support of science and fossil research in Thailand.

The molar is 0.46 inch (11.56 millimeters) long and almost as wide. That sounds small. It isn’t small next to the teeth of its relatives.

According to recent reports, yakamys belongs to Ischyromyidae, one of the earliest major families of rodents. Its molar is the largest yet described among early members of that family.

It has been revealed that until now, an animal called Hulgana was regarded as the largest Asian member of the family. Its molars are less than half as long and less than half as wide.

Industry observers note that the closest in size is Manitsha tanka. This rodent was described from South Dakota in 1941. Its lower second molar measures about 0.32 by 0.35 inch (8.2 by 8.9 millimeters).

The incisor was cut lengthwise by the team to place Yakamys in that family. Its enamel was then examined under an electron microscope.

The banding inside the enamel is consistent with the pattern reported for other members of the family.

No bones of Yakamys have been found and so its weight had to be estimated from tooth measurements.

Bigger teeth go with heavier bodies in living rodents and this relationship has been turned into equations.

Virginie Millien is a biologist at McGill University in Canada. She applied seven published equations to the two teeth. The answers ranged from 47 to 104 pounds (21.4 to 47.3 kilograms).

The seven answers averaged 70 pounds (31.6 kilograms) and the middle value was 63 pounds (28.6 kilograms).

The team took the midpoint of those two figures and rounded it to 30 kilograms, or 66 pounds.

Industry observers note that the weight reported by the team is therefore a rounded summary of answers that disagree. Millien called it “only a ballpark figure.”.

Estimates of this kind are uncertain because the link between tooth size and body weight varies among living rodents. The estimates span roughly 24 to 152 pounds (10.8 to 69 kilograms) when each margin of error is included.

Recent findings suggest that the weights of giant rodents have been revised sharply before. One South American giant was first estimated at more than 2,200 pounds (1,000 kilograms).

Later studies that included one by Millien in 2008 estimated about 770 pounds (350 kilograms).

It has been revealed that rodents include more species than any other group of living mammals. Their oldest fossils come from North America. Very large body size has evolved in only a few branches of the group.

In a recent development, the best-known giants lived in South America long after Yakamys. Large species were rarely documented among early rodents and Manitsha was one of the few examples.

The fossil record of the family in Asia was sparse. Most of it came from small animals in China and India.

Yakamys extends the known range of the family into Southeast Asia. It is also evidence that one early rodent line had already grown large by about 34 million years ago.

According to recent reports, yakamys and Manitsha are similar in estimated weight but their molars are built differently. To the authors, that suggests large size in this family wasn’t tied to one tooth design.

Giant rodents are commonly linked to life on islands. That explanation is hard to apply to Yakamys.

The authors wrote that the ancient geography of the Krabi area doesn’t point to an island. Neither do the other mammals found there.

The clay that held the teeth formed in a lake. Many other fossil mammals have been found in the coal around it.

It has been revealed that one possibility was raised by the team. Yakamys may have lived along lake edges much as capybaras live near water today. Food there may have been plentiful.

But lake clay alone doesn’t show that an animal spent time in the water.

More complete fossils that include skull and skeleton bones would be needed to test the idea. More evidence from the rocks and the other animals at the site would be needed too.

Two teeth aren’t enough to establish exactly where Yakamys belongs within its family. The researchers could not run a formal analysis to identify its closest relatives.

Industry observers note that even the pairing of the teeth is tentative. The molar and the incisor were found close together in the same layer. The team assigned both to one species because both are unusually large.

A 3D model of the molar is available through MorphoMuseuM, an open online collection of 3D specimens. Other researchers can examine the tooth there.

Yakamys may not have been the first large rodent in the region.

An unpublished rodent incisor from older rocks in Myanmar is held by the same team. It is considerably larger than the incisors of other rodents described from the region.

In a recent development, the Myanmar incisor hasn’t been formally described or identified. Its size alone can’t show what kind of rodent it came from.

According to recent reports, one question remains open. Was large body size a local event or a more widespread part of early rodent evolution?

More fossils from Myanmar and elsewhere in the region will be needed to answer it.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Starting in 2027, the Genting Dream will get a dedicated fashion retail space, which will feature a collection of fashion and lifestyle pieces and exclusive merchandise available only onboard.

The collaboration will also bring fashion reveals and designer showcases to the ship, opening up upcoming opportunities for Chinese designers and original brands to introduce their work to consumers across Southeast Asia, according to a statement.

StarDream Cruises President Michael Goh and LOTI Co-Founder Pan YuanYua signed the agreement in Singapore on November 13.

“Cruising is about creating memorable experiences, and we are always looking at fresh ways to bring fresh and exciting lifestyle offerings onboard for our guests,” noted Goh.

In a recent development, “Through our collaboration with LOTI, we look forward to bringing a new fashion experience to Genting Dream, from exclusive merchandise and curated collections to designer showcases at sea. The collaboration brings together travel and fashion, creating latest ways for guests to discover and engage with creativity throughout their holiday.

Sources indicate that “LOTI has always been committed to bringing original Chinese design to the global stage. Through this collaboration with Dream Cruises’ Genting Dream, we are taking the fashion runway to the sea,” noted Yuanyuan.

“Leveraging the unique advantage of a cruise voyage that connects destinations across Southeast Asia, we have created an immersive maritime fashion space that integrates retail, fashion showcases, and exclusive products, allowing guests from around the world to experience the charm of Chinese design while on holiday.”.

The Genting Dream operates  two-, three- and five-night cruises year-round from Singapore and Malaysia, taking guests to destinations across Southeast Asia, including Kuala Lumpur, Melaka, Penang and Redang Island in Malaysia; Phuket, Bangkok and Koh Samui in Thailand; and Bali in Indonesia.

Can DC’s new delegate get Congress to care about statehood?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when Robert White gets sworn into Congress on Jan.
  • Recent findings suggest that as Democrats look forward to life in the majority, they’ve got big plans as they try to deliver on their affordability campaign promises and conduct oversight of the Trump administration.
  • Recent findings suggest that “The agenda gets done if you have the votes — and D.C.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when Robert White gets sworn into Congress on Jan. 3, he’ll have one thing on his mind: convincing the rest of his party that D.C. statehood belongs on the priority list.

Recent findings suggest that as Democrats look forward to life in the majority, they’ve got big plans as they try to deliver on their affordability campaign promises and conduct oversight of the Trump administration. White, a 44-year-old former councilmember who was born and raised in the District, has his pitch ready.

Recent findings suggest that “The agenda gets done if you have the votes — and D.C. statehood gives you more votes,” he remarked.

His election marks a fresh chapter for the District’s nonvoting delegate. As Eleanor Holmes Norton retires after more than three decades, he’ll be just the third person to hold the seat in modern times. It also comes as President Donald Trump has tried to exert more control over local affairs in the nation’s capital.

White has the delicate task of paying homage to the legacy of his former boss (he once worked as her legislative counsel) while also putting some distance between them. Norton was known as a fierce advocate for the District but lately appeared to struggle through prepared remarks as her influence diminished. Earlier in her time in Congress, she pushed through both concrete and symbolic incremental wins, such as securing delegates the right to vote in what’s known as the committee of the whole.

He said Norton “built powerfully” on the work of Walter Fauntroy, who served as delegate from 1971 to 1991. “And my job is to build on top of what Norton built.”.

At a Monday event, White’s father, Robert White Sr., wore a shirt with a slogan to that effect: “FAUNTROY & NORTON & WHITE.”.

A crowd was assembled outside the John A. Wilson Building that night to mark White’s departure from the D.C. Council, after a last-minute uproar over a provision in the 1970 law establishing D.C.’s delegate position. Although he had hoped to serve on the council until January, the law states a delegate must hold “no other paid public office” on the date of his election, and White ultimately decided to resign before Election Day. As he stepped up to the podium, someone shouted a rallying cry that has only grown louder after Trump deployed National Guard troops to patrol the streets last year: “Free D.C.”.

According to recent reports, white won’t be the only freshman member next Congress who can’t cast a vote on the House floor — Alicia Limtiaco is another newcomer, after beating incumbent Del. James Moylan in Guam.

One way White thinks he can further his cause is by boosting his own name recognition.

Sources indicate that “I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he stated. “I’ve got to hire the right comms director with the experience to help me get it done. I’m going to use the proximity of my seat here in D.C., making sure that all the national outlets know that when other members go back to their district, I’m still here and available to do interviews. Everything that we can do, including building relationships in other media markets, including through my leadership PAC, we’re going to be doing.”.

He aims to start making his case before the new Congress even begins.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m already starting to put together materials for all incoming members, and talking to leadership to see if I can carve out a piece of fresh member orientation to talk about D.C. both being a resource to members while they’re here, but also D.C. statehood,” he said.

In a recent development, he knows that even in his own party, standing up for D.C. can be a tough sell. A number of moderate Democrats have voted with Republicans on bills seeking to undermine D.C.’s autonomy and roll back local criminal justice laws over the last few years.

“We have seen D.C. used as a bargaining chip by the party,” he said. “The Democratic Party has not consistently been a firewall for D.C.”.

According to recent reports, party consensus on D.C. statehood has evolved over time, but it hasn’t always been a unifying concern. In 1993, 105 House Democrats joined 172 Republicans in voting against a bill from Norton that would have paved the way for statehood and for the addition of two senators and a representative in Congress. When the House voted on statehood bills again in 2020 and 2021, it passed with near-unanimous Democratic support but stalled in the Senate.

Asked how he would respond to Democratic peers in Congress who might say they support D.C. statehood but need to focus first on concerns like affordability that more directly affect their constituents, White countered with a question of his own.

“How’s that been going without the two senators from the District of Columbia?” he said.

He sees parallels with Republicans using redistricting to gain seats in Congress.

“People need to say to their constituents, ‘Look, not only are we doing what is right under democracy, but we are helping get the votes for our agenda.’ That is what the Republicans tried to do with redistricting. So, if you think you’re going to keep playing around the margins and start winning when that hasn’t worked, we’re fooling ourselves,” he said.

Industry observers note that the way White sees it, appeals to the principles of democracy still ring true when arguing for full representation for the District’s some 700,000 residents. But pragmatic arguments matter, too.

Industry observers note that “When they see D.C. statehood as their ticket to securing reproductive rights, their ticket to being able to afford health health care, then they start to see D.C statehood in a different light — and that is the light that I want to make sure I’m putting on this issue now,” he said.

#30870. Protecting forest birds may depend on what happens outside park boundaries

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1290 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Protecting forest birds may depend on what happens outside park boundaries

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Forest birds in small national park sites may depend as much on surrounding forests as on habitat within park boundaries, a new study suggests.
  • In a recent development, drawing the boundaries of a national park on a map is easy.
  • Forest birds such as thrushes, warblers, and woodpeckers may build their nests inside national parks, but they often depend on the land outside those parks too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forest birds in small national park sites may depend as much on surrounding forests as on habitat within park boundaries, a new study suggests.

In a recent development, drawing the boundaries of a national park on a map is easy. Trees stay where they grow, but birds don’t follow those boundaries.

Forest birds such as thrushes, warblers, and woodpeckers may build their nests inside national parks, but they often depend on the land outside those parks too.

Researchers examined eight small national park sites in the northeastern United States, comparing forest characteristics inside each park with those in the surrounding county.

Bird presence inside the parks was associated with forest characteristics across the surrounding county at least as strongly as with those across the park itself.

Small parks are therefore unlikely to protect forest birds without help from the land around them.

It has been revealed that the analysis was carried out by Bruna Amaral, who is a doctoral student at Michigan State University. Her collaborator Elise Zipkin is an ecologist who heads the university’s Ecology, Evolution, and Behavior program.

Sources indicate that sixteen species were included in the work. The researchers asked only whether each species was present at a given survey point.

It has been revealed that bird numbers and nesting success were not followed. The results therefore describe a pattern and cannot be used to prove a cause.

Sources indicate that surveys were conducted each May and June between 2006 and 2023. Volunteers with the National Park Service’s Northeast Temperate Network visited fixed points in the forest of every park.

At each point, an observer spent ten minutes recording every bird within 164 feet (50 meters).

According to recent reports, roughly 91% of the records came from birds identified by their sound. Only those sound records were used in the analysis.

Recent findings suggest that all 16 species are classed as forest birds. The wood thrush, the ovenbird, the scarlet tanager, and several warblers are included among them.

According to recent reports, the parks were not created for wildlife. They are national historic sites and historical parks whose main purpose is the preservation of history.

The smallest park covers only 69 acres (28 hectares), which is close to the area of 50 football fields. About 2,860 acres (1,156 hectares) are covered by the largest park.

Acadia National Park was excluded from the study. One reason given was that it is more than ten times larger than the other parks.

Sources indicate that which forest was most closely tied to the presence of each bird? That was the question put to the data.

Three candidates were considered. The first was the forest within a quarter mile (400 meters) of the survey point. The whole park was the second, and the surrounding county was the third.

Five measures were used to describe the forest at each scale. Among them were conifer amount, shrub cover, and the number of large old trees.

Because a bird feeds, nests, and hides in the nearest forest, the team had expected it to matter most.

The researchers identified 40 statistically significant associations between bird presence and forest characteristics, involving 13 of the 16 species.

According to recent reports, county forest accounted for 19 of the 40 links. Another 16 links were to the forest near the survey point. Only five were to the park as a whole.

Recent findings suggest that so the forest averaged across a whole park revealed the fewest links of the three. That is the very area a boundary defines.

It has been revealed that the authors described the county result as surprising. These parks hold older and more varied forest than the land around them.

Three species were linked only to county forest. They were the wood thrush, the scarlet tanager, and the brown creeper.

Bark is where a brown creeper finds its food. The small brown-and-white bird climbs tree trunks in a spiral and pulls insects from the cracks.

Creepers were more likely to be present in a park when its county’s forests had more or bigger trees.

Recent findings suggest that fewer shrubs in those county forests were also tied to their presence. Inside the parks, no forest measure showed a reliable link to the bird.

“Species rarely respect human-made boundaries,” the authors wrote.

Sources indicate that the forest close to each survey point was linked to ten species. Different species, however, were linked to different kinds of forest.

In a recent development, the black-throated blue warbler nests in shrubs. It was more likely to be present where shrub cover was thick and large old trees were fewer.

Downy woodpeckers dig their nest holes in decayed wood. These birds were more likely to be present where large old trees were plentiful and conifers were scarce.

Downy woodpeckers occurred in every park where black-throated blue warblers were recorded, suggesting those parks contain forest conditions suitable for both species.

Recent findings suggest that only weak, mixed links were found between park size and the birds. Five species were more likely to be present in bigger parks, and two were less likely. No pattern at all was seen for most species.

The team didn’t test why county forest would be tied to the birds inside a park.

Sources indicate that one possible reason lies in the weeks after young birds leave the nest, Amaral said. Survival in that period depends partly on the land a young bird moves through before migrating south.

In a recent development, earlier research on wood thrushes found that young birds do move this way. Mature forest is left behind for younger woods with dense undergrowth.

There the young thrushes eat insects and fruit and hide from predators.

Recent findings suggest that edges are another possibility. More forest edge is found in a county with broken-up forest, and nest predators are more active at edges.

Birds returning from migration may also pick a region first. A nesting territory would then be chosen second.

In a recent development, the land around the eight parks varies widely. Minute Man National Historical Park in Massachusetts lies in an open, broken-up landscape.

Marsh-Billings-Rockefeller National Historical Park in Vermont, by contrast, lies in a broadly forested county.

“We need to start to think beyond park boundaries,” Amaral remarked.

Benefits from bird-friendly backyards and farms can reach the parks next to them, Zipkin remarked.

It has been revealed that conservation easements were also suggested by the team. These are legal agreements that limit development on private land. They may be easier to arrange than enlarging a park.

Industry observers note that the counts show whether a species was present. Once birds arrive, their nesting success may still be shaped by the park’s own forest, the authors wrote.

In a recent development, only one park-wide value and one county value per forest measure came from each park. Estimates at those two scales are therefore less precise than the estimates for nearby forest.

Sources indicate that what the measures capture is the kind of forest found in a county. How much forest a county holds was not part of them.

Every one of the eight parks is small, and about 60% of the surrounding region is still forest. No data on bird population trends in the surrounding counties were available to the team.

Trends inside and outside the parks could therefore not be compared.

Sources indicate that the authors identified a next step: testing whether a park’s surroundings influence how birds respond to forest conditions inside it. This could help managers apply the findings.

The full study was published in the journal Landscape Ecology.

Breaking: Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (630 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.
  • It has been revealed that the well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

It has been revealed that the well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

Sources indicate that in patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

In a recent development, chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

It has been revealed that for the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is key because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

It has been revealed that researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

Recent findings suggest that the team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

It has been revealed that the researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle states, patients’ damaged kidneys demonstrated clear signs of repair.

October broke a global heat record, and El Niño is still strengthening

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • October 2026 was the warmest October on record, as an intensifying El Niño added to global warmth and ocean temperatures reached newly introduced highs.
  • The global average surface air temperature in October 2026 was 15.35°C.
  • That’s 0.90°C above the 1991–2020 average and enough to make it the warmest October in the ERA5 record, beating October 2023 by 0.05°C.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October 2026 was the warmest October on record, as an intensifying El Niño added to global warmth and ocean temperatures reached newly introduced highs.

The global average surface air temperature in October 2026 was 15.35°C.

That’s 0.90°C above the 1991–2020 average and enough to make it the warmest October in the ERA5 record, beating October 2023 by 0.05°C.

It was also 1.75°C above the estimated pre-industrial baseline.

Recent findings suggest that the data come from the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the European Union’s climate monitoring service. And the numbers keep stacking.

In a recent development, before August 2026, the last individual month above 1.5°C was November 2025. Then August, September and October crossed it.

The last streak of three or more consecutive months above 1.5°C ended in April 2025.

The rolling twelve-month average – November 2025 through October 2026 – now sits at 1.51°C above pre-industrial levels.

January through October 2026 ranks as the second-warmest such period on record, 0.07°C below the same stretch in 2024 and 0.05°C above 2023.

A statistical model trained on 1979–2025 data gives 2026 a greater than 99% chance of exceeding 1.5°C for the full calendar year. That would make it only the second calendar year above that level after 2024.

There’s roughly an 80% probability it finishes as the second-warmest year on record and about a 20% chance it ties or exceeds 2024 for the top spot.

If 2026 does exceed 1.5°C, the four-year average for 2023–2026 would also cross that line.

According to recent reports, an intensifying El Niño is adding to the global warmth. Sea surface temperatures across 60°S–60°N hit 20.95°C in October.

This is the highest October value ever recorded. The previous October record was set in 2023 during a developing El Niño. This one is considerably stronger.

It has been revealed that the Niño 3.4 region – the patch of equatorial Pacific used to define El Niño intensity – averaged 29.94°C in October. That’s an all-time high for the region in any month, surpassing the record set just one month earlier in September.

Industry observers note that the anomaly was +3.21°C, also a record, above September’s +2.99°C. For context, this exceeds the peaks of the monster El Niños of 1982–83, 1997–98, and 2015–16.

Across much of the central equatorial Pacific, temperatures ran more than 3°C above average. Along the Peruvian coast and west of the Galápagos, the anomalies reached 6 to 7°C.

The World Meteorological Organization expects this El Niño to peak in December 2026 and to persist through at least February 2027.

The ocean heat isn’t confined to the Pacific. Record October sea surface temperatures were also logged in parts of the northern Indian Ocean, the South Atlantic, and the subtropical North Atlantic.

Around Europe, records fell along the Atlantic coast and in the central and western Mediterranean.

The largest land-based anomalies on the planet were over West Antarctica.

There, temperatures ran more than 7°C above the October average and reached up to 11°C above normal in some areas.

The Copernicus report links this to high pressure over the Drake Passage and a wave pattern typically associated with El Niño. Siberia, the central United States, northern Canada, eastern Africa, and the Middle East also ran warm.

Cold anomalies demonstrated up across much of southern South America, Greenland, northern Africa, parts of central Asia, and western Australia.

Recent findings suggest that the warmth was not everywhere. But it was dominant.

European land temperatures averaged 11.08°C – 1.49°C above normal and the second-warmest October in the ERA5 record, behind only October 2022.

But unlike the record-breaking summer and September, the warmth was unevenly distributed.

Northern Fennoscandia and far-eastern Europe saw the most extreme departures, with Ukraine reaching up to 6°C above average.

Western Europe, by contrast, hovered closer to normal. Southern Italy, the southern Balkans, Greece, the eastern Mediterranean, and western Türkiye were actually about 2°C below average.

According to recent reports, individual months above 1.5°C are not the same as the sustained, multi-decadal average the Paris Agreement refers to. But the frequency with which individual months are crossing the threshold keeps increasing.

It has been revealed that the first calendar year above 1.5°C happened in 2024. The second is almost certainly happening now.

A four-year average above 1.5°C would be another sign that the world is nearing the Paris Agreement’s long-term warming limit.

El Niño is expected to strengthen further before peaking in December, keeping attention on how this exceptional year will end.

Industry News: Protecting cities from floods can come with a hidden cost for renters

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Flood protection projects in Copenhagen may raise rents and water bills unevenly, placing a heavier burden on lower-income tenants.
  • A city can become better protected against flooding while becoming more expensive for its poorest residents.
  • New research shows how drainage projects can leave tenants paying disproportionately through higher rents and water bills.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Flood protection projects in Copenhagen may raise rents and water bills unevenly, placing a heavier burden on lower-income tenants.

A city can become better protected against flooding while becoming more expensive for its poorest residents.

New research shows how drainage projects can leave tenants paying disproportionately through higher rents and water bills.

The study, led by researchers at the University of Copenhagen, examined how flood protection costs reach households across the Danish capital.

Lead author Natalie Marie Gulsrud and her colleagues combined geographical analysis with a detailed look at the Hørgården housing development.

Their findings show why a policy applied equally on paper can feel very different depending on where someone lives.

At Hørgården, roughly 60 percent of residents have incomes below the Danish average. The development also appears on the Ministry of Social Affairs and Housing’s Prevention Areas list.

Industry observers note that its aging sewers need repairs, and a planned cloudburst route brings another obligation. Rainwater draining from roofs must be separated from wastewater and connected to the new system.

The paper projects rent increases of 17%–29% for the combined work. For a 75-square-meter apartment, that would add 967–1,292 Danish kroner to the monthly bill.

Sources indicate that stormwater separation accounts for about 22% of that increase, or 213–284 kroner each month. Most of the increase comes from sewer repairs.

Industry observers note that the loans will be repaid over 30 years. Residents moving into Hørgården years after the work is finished will therefore help pay for it.

Sources indicate that copenhagen is investing in cloudburst tunnels and drainage improvements to keep heavy rain from overwhelming its sewers. Separating stormwater from wastewater is part of that effort.

The work protects the city, but apartment residents and not-for-profit tenants can bear a disproportionate share of its financing.

“Climate adaptation is not only about flooding and sewer capacity. It is also about rising rents,” Gulsrud said.

In a recent development, “Your type of housing determines how much of the bill you pay. Our case study demonstrates that one-size-fits-all climate adaptation policies worsen urban injustice.”.

“Stormwater costs fall disproportionately on not-for-profit housing residents, despite Copenhagen’s reputation for climate leadership.”.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers compared adaptation plans with data on housing types and tenure. They found that not-for-profit housing often lies closer to priority areas for flood management.

That proximity matters because properties along a cloudburst route may have to change their drainage systems at their own expense.

“We can see that not-for-profit housing is often located where cloudburst routes are typically established,” Gulsrud explained.

Sources indicate that “The problem arises when properties along these routes are required to separate stormwater from wastewater on their own land to connect it to the cloudburst system. This makes sense from a water-management perspective, but it can also impose substantial costs.”.

In a recent development, for an older development such as Hørgården, connecting to the new infrastructure involves extensive work. Those expenses ultimately reach households through their rents.

Water bills introduce a separate problem. Stormwater charges are based on drinking water consumption in each dwelling, rather than the rainwater leaving the property.

Imagine a detached house beside a four-storey block containing four apartments. Both buildings have a 100-square-meter roof.

According to recent reports, if every household uses the same amount of drinking water, the apartment block pays four times the stormwater charge. Its roof is no larger.

This arrangement disadvantages buildings where many households share a roof. Not-for-profit developments commonly have four to six storeys.

“It would be fair if payment reflected the amount of stormwater each property actually discharges into the sewer system,” Gulsrud noted.

“At present, charges are tied to drinking water consumption instead. There is a fundamental inequity in the way water bills are allocated and in how residents pay for climate adaptation and cloudburst management.”.

“As water charges continue to rise, the burden falls most heavily on the most marginalised members of society.”.

In a recent development, the researchers also examined how these decisions are made. They found a divide between departments responsible for technical infrastructure and those dealing with social policy.

That leaves household finances poorly accounted for when drainage requirements are enforced. A project can satisfy engineering standards while putting residents under greater financial strain.

“In this paper we hope to introduce a human aspect to a highly technical topic involving stormwater pipes, housing tenure, and climate financing,” Gulsrud remarked.

According to recent reports, in Hørgården, public records demonstrated that officials knew housing costs would rise. Those costs nevertheless did not determine whether the separation requirement would go ahead.

It has been revealed that the authors argue that closer cooperation between social and technical departments could help distribute costs more fairly. Housing circumstances and household resources would then become part of planning the work.

For residents, that would mean considering the rent bill alongside the drainage initiative.

Industry observers note that “Who gets protected as the climate changes, and who carries the cost? A just transition needs social and technical governance working together, not on separate tracks.”.

“If we don’t fix this, we risk deepening socio ecological inequalities in the green transition. We hope this research moves us closer to a transition that is genuinely just and caring,” Gulsrud concluded.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Associated Press call came at 1:26 a.m.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Democrats seized control of the House on Tuesday by safeguarding vulnerable incumbents and flipping districts in both battleground and deep-red terrain, delivering a sweeping repudiation of Donald Trump and Republicans that threatens to stall the president’s remaining agenda.

The Associated Press call came at 1:26 a.m. Eastern time Wednesday, hours after Democrats were projected to win a majority in the Senate, with a string of victories in deeply conservative states.

In a recent development, “The American people have spoken and made clear they've had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,’’ House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black speaker, told cheering supporters in Washington. “They want a Congress that's going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do.”.

Recent findings suggest that recent polls had forecast a strong Democratic showing amid rising discontent with the president's policies and economic anxiety driven by rising prices and the Iran war. But the magnitude of the Democratic majority surprised even the most optimistic Democratic partisans.

The “blue tsunami” marked an extraordinary turnaround for a party that suffered withering losses in 2024, when Trump returned to the White House and Republicans won a governing trifecta in Washington.

Recent findings suggest that republicans had hoped that a mid-decade redistricting push driven by Trump would help them keep their majority by flipping House seats in Texas, North Carolina, Florida and Ohio, among other states. Instead, many of those districts remained in Democrats’ hands.

Trump put himself front and center of the midterm campaign, imploring voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” On Tuesday, he posted on social media that he “wasn’t on the ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”.

But in a later interview with CBS News, Trump congratulated Democrats on their rout. “My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country," he noted.

Industry observers note that among the night’s Democratic pickups were seats in rural and Republican-leaning districts. Farmer Jamie Ager defeated Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to flip a Western North Carolina seat that was left open after Republican Chuck Edwards declared his retirement after facing allegations of sexual harassment.

Industry observers note that in Kentucky’s 6th District, Democrat Zach Dembo, a Navy veteran and former federal prosecutor, defeated former state Sen. Ralph Alvarado for an open seat anchored in Lexington.

Industry observers note that democrats also swept perennial battleground districts, flipping seats in states such as Upcoming Jersey, Colorado and Wisconsin. And in Pennsylvania, Democrats were projected to flip all four seats they were targeting, including the Philadelphia-area district of GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.

According to recent reports, anger over Trump’s tariff policy drove discontent in farm country, with Democrats ousting Republican Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa and flipping the seat of Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson, who lost her bid to succeed retiring Sen. Joni Ernst.

Meanwhile, Latino voters, who were credited with helping propel Trump back into the White House in 2024, bolstered Democratic successes in Texas, scuttling GOP hopes of making good on the party’s mid-decade redistricting gambit.

Texas Republicans believed Latino voters would stick with the party this year when they redrew the state's congressional map to create up to five pickup opportunities. But anger over the president’s immigration policies, coupled with economic anxiety, has driven Trump’s approval numbers among Latinos to historic lows.

Recent findings suggest that in South Texas, a pair of Democratic incumbents — Reps. Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar — easily held on to their redrawn seats, while former Bexar County sheriff's deputy Johnny Garcia prevailed over Air Force veteran Carlos De La Cruz in a district newly redrawn to elect a Republican. Democratic attorney and educator Katy Padilla Stout flipped the open 23rd District, which stretches across the state’s border with Mexico, and Tejano singer Bobby Pulido routed GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in another South Texas race.

In a recent development, the strength of the Democrats’ performance was evident in several under-the-radar races the party won in traditionally red districts, including Missouri’s 2nd District, where Republican Rep. Ann Wagner was ousted, and Indiana’s 5th, where Rep. Victoria Spartz lost reelection.

Speaker Mike Johnson, who crisscrossed the country to boost Republican candidates in the final weeks of the campaign, noted Tuesday night that history wasn’t on the GOP side: The president’s party almost always loses seats in a midterm election.

It has been revealed that "From the first day of this election, we knew that to keep the House and sustain our majority we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history," Johnson stated in Shreveport, La. "It looks like history will be kept tonight.".

The new Democratic majority is expected to dedicate resources to investigating the activities of the Trump administration as well as the president.

The likely new Democratic chairman of the House Judiciary Committee is Maryland’s Jamie Raskin, while the Oversight and Government Reform panel is likely to be led by California Rep. Robert Garcia. Raskin and Garcia have already been busy making oversight requests of the administration.

For instance, the two lawmakers joined on a letter last week calling for the retention of conversations between the president and AI chatbots on matters of policy.

Recent findings suggest that "The President and his advisors’ use of AI exposes the country to malign influence from unknown and unaccountable third parties. We already have ample evidence that AI chatbots can be manipulated to suit the commercial, political, or personal agendas of their designers​," Raskin and Garcia wrote.

Beyond the oversight, Jeffries outlined last month some of his legislative priorities for the next Congress.

"I think we need to put money in the pockets of everyday Americans by doing things like expanding the Child Tax Credit, as well as the Earned Income Tax Credit​," Jeffries told News12. "And, of course, we also need to end this war because the war has dramatically increased gas prices, fertilizer prices and diesel costs.​".

That was a reference to the military campaign against Iran, which appears likely to ratchet back up after the midterms.

I​n a pre-election interview with CNN, Jeffries noted priorities that unite the Democratic Caucus include action on stopping the president's sweeping application of tariffs, as well as on reversing cuts to Medicaid and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits.
