Latest Update: Lasers and robots using AI are launching a third revolution in farming by completely changing how we kill weeds

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1158 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lasers, robots and spot sprayers cut herbicide use, but two weed scientists explain why herbicide resistance will keep evolving around them.
  • In theory, a machine that rolls through a farm to zap or dig up individual weeds should be the perfect way to eliminate harmful chemicals and stop chemical-resistant weeds in their tracks.
  • However, two scientists recently warned that this high-tech farming dream is not yet the absolute cure everyone hopes it will be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lasers, robots and spot sprayers cut herbicide use, but two weed scientists explain why herbicide resistance will keep evolving around them.

In theory, a machine that rolls through a farm to zap or dig up individual weeds should be the perfect way to eliminate harmful chemicals and stop chemical-resistant weeds in their tracks.

However, two scientists recently warned that this high-tech farming dream is not yet the absolute cure everyone hopes it will be.

Recent findings suggest that resistance comes from the weeds that are hit and survive, not from how much herbicide the field gets. So a machine that treats only the weeds can cut herbicide use sharply and still favor resistant plants just as strongly.

The warning comes in a commentary by Lynn Sosnoskie of Cornell University and Stephen Duke of the University of Mississippi.

It’s an assessment of what the upcoming machines have done so far, with no new field experiments of its own. It weighs the benefits against the trouble that the two scientists expect will follow.

“In the last 100 years, there have been two revolutions in weed management: synthetic herbicides and herbicide-resistant crops,” said Duke, a research professor at the University’s National Center for Natural Products Research.

“It looks to me like AI-driven precision weed management will be the next revolution.”.

The machines come in three kinds, and all start with a camera. Software picks weeds out from crop plants and bare soil as the machine moves. Most carry their own lights under a hood, so they can work at night.

A sprayer then hits each weed with a nozzle, a laser burns its growing point, or a cultivator pulls it out.

The savings can be real. In U.S. trials of the one spot-spraying system, herbicide savings averaged about $50 an acre ($123 a hectare) in soybeans and $17 an acre ($43 a hectare) in corn.

In vegetable trials that Sosnoskie ran, laser weeding caused almost no crop injury, left the crop plants at least 30 percent heavier, and matched the yields of weed-free plots.

Sosnoskie, an associate professor in Cornell’s School of Integrative Plant Science, works on fruit and vegetable crops, and she remarked herbicides can damage or stunt them.

“But what we’re finding is that with precision technology, we can keep some, and sometimes even all, of the herbicide off the crop,” she added.

Some commercial robotic weeders run about $75,000 or more, and laser systems can cost over $1 million.

According to recent reports, one U.S. analysis estimated that a spot-sprayer pays for itself in saved herbicide only after treating about 53,000 to 116,000 acres (21,500 to 47,000 hectares). Where the area falls, within that range, depends on weed density and herbicide prices.

Duke described an organic farmer in the Netherlands who bought a laser weeder for more than a million dollars. It saved the farmer so much hassle that he bought a second one, Duke noted, but that won’t be true for everyone.

“Some of these farmers who are working with high-value crops can spend that much, but many can’t.”.

Sources indicate that organic growers have a particular reason, Duke stated. They can’t use synthetic herbicides, so they depend on hand weeding, and that labor is getting harder to find.

Prices are expected to fall as production scales up, the authors wrote, and some systems may be retrofitted onto existing equipment.

Farmers worldwide spend an estimated $35 billion to $47 billion a year on herbicides, and the authors wrote that wide adoption of these machines could shrink that market.

Fewer sales could mean less money for finding latest herbicides, which are already scarce. Few substances with a new mode of action have reached the market in four decades, even as public pressure builds against chemicals such as glyphosate, the most widely used of them.

It has been revealed that the weed resistance problem is subtler. A weed becomes resistant when a treated plant survives and reproduces, so what matters is what happens to each sprayed plant, not how much herbicide the field gets.

Industry observers note that A camera that misses a weed leaves it untreated, and a nozzle that only partly covers one gives it a low dose. The authors wrote that both could speed up resistance rather than slow it down.

Fast growers such as Palmer amaranth and waterhemp can quickly outgrow the size a sprayer handles after a missed pass, and each plant can drop hundreds of thousands of seeds.

“That doesn’t mean every weed is resistant to every herbicide, but there are a lot of herbicide-resistant weeds out there,” Duke said. “It’s become a really major problem.”.

Industry observers note that the second warning is about the camera itself. A weed that sprouts under the crop canopy, grows in an unusual shape or looks enough like the crop stands a better chance of being left alone. Over many seasons, that could select for weeds that are harder to spot.

According to recent reports, weeds have done this before. Under generations of hand weeding, a barnyard grass that grows in rice paddies evolved a more upright shape and a white central vein on its leaf.

Recent findings suggest that both are features of cultivated rice, so farmers pulled it less often. The authors called a repeat under machine vision speculative but plausible.

Recent findings suggest that lasers and cultivators favor a different set of weeds, because both attack only the part of the plant above ground. Perennials that regrow from roots, tubers or underground stems could come to dominate fields where those machines do most of the work.

Recent findings suggest that “What I’ve been arguing is just because we have this technology, that doesn’t free us from weeds,” Sosnoskie noted. “With weed control, we always have to think about how the weed is going to respond or try to ‘win.'”.

According to recent reports, the software is only as good as the pictures it learned from. Dust, crop residue, odd lighting and a stressed crop that looks like a weed can all throw off the system.

“I worked with a manufacturer whose original algorithm kept missing one specific weed species: common ragweed,” Sosnoskie said. “Well, it turns out they don’t have the same ragweed species in California.”.

The authors’ own conclusion is blunt. Weeds evolved around herbicides, and they expect weeds to evolve around the new machines too. Which traits, and how fast, is still speculation.

The systems will also need better sensors and more varied training images to hold their accuracy from one region to the next, they wrote.

Sources indicate that furthermore, the old, soil-applied herbicides that stop weeds before they sprout are likely to stay in use alongside the farm AI. Fewer weeds coming up means fewer for a camera to miss.

The full study was published in the journal Engineering.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

In a recent development, but the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

It has been revealed that global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite massive enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”.

It has been revealed that for the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters states. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”.

#30860. Top-ranking parakeets face a hostile welcome after time away

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1201 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Top-ranking parakeets face a hostile welcome after time away

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1201 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Monk parakeets change their fighting habits when dominant birds leave, often bullying them when they return to the flock.
  • When a high-ranking monk parakeet disappears from its flock, the other birds adjust to its absence.
  • Researchers kept some high-ranking birds away from their flocks for eight days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Monk parakeets change their fighting habits when dominant birds leave, often bullying them when they return to the flock.

When a high-ranking monk parakeet disappears from its flock, the other birds adjust to its absence. But a fresh study shows that its return can trigger a shift toward bullying.

Researchers kept some high-ranking birds away from their flocks for eight days.

When they returned, most were bullied by the other birds. They were attacked much more often than they attacked others.

The work was led by Annemarie van der Marel while she was a postdoctoral researcher in Elizabeth Hobson’s lab at the University of Cincinnati.

Van der Marel now works at the Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity in Chile.

Monk parakeets are highly social parrots. They ease into friendships and they spend much of their time squabbling.

According to recent reports, every bird in the study was held in captivity. The researchers counted fights over space. In each one, a parakeet moved in on another bird, which then gave up its spot.

Between 2020 and 2022, 51 monk parakeets were observed in four flocks. The birds were kept in flight pens in Gainesville, Florida. The pens belong to the USDA National Wildlife Research Center.

In a recent development, most of the birds had been caught in southern Florida. The species comes from South America but now lives wild in that region.

Observers logged more than 118,000 contests over about 1,460 hours.

“Each bird received a color mark so that we could identify them individually. We all had our favorites. They have a lot of personality,” van der Marel stated.

According to recent reports, every three days, the wins and losses were used to rank the birds. In this way, the researchers worked out each flock’s pecking order.

In three of the flocks, one bird at a time was then removed. Each bird was chosen for its rank and housed apart for eight days. It was then returned to the same pen.

Fifteen birds went through that cycle. Nine of them ranked at or near the top of their flock. The other six held middle or lower ranks.

Three fighting patterns were described in a 2021 study by Hobson and two colleagues. Each pattern reflects how the members of an animal group pick their opponents.

In the first pattern, an animal attacks any lower-ranked group member.

Recent findings suggest that in the second, it mostly attacks rivals ranked just below it. The third pattern, called bullying, involves mostly attacking group members ranked much lower.

According to recent reports, each undisturbed flock maintained its existing fighting pattern. One flock showed bullying for as long as it was watched.

Another flock attacked any bird of lower rank during the month before its removals. That pattern was not changed by a thunderstorm.

It was also not changed when two injured birds were taken out for care. A change of partner by the top-ranked bird had no effect either.

According to recent reports, the patterns began to change once the removals started. Sixteen switches were recorded immediately after a bird was removed or returned.

Recent findings suggest that other switches were recorded between those events. No switch was recorded after some of the removals and returns. A group changing its pattern over time had not been documented before, the authors wrote.

A returning bird loses its rank according to the team’s earlier study.

The researchers therefore expected the other birds to have little reason to change how they fought.

The flock’s fighting pattern changed after six of the nine top-ranked birds were removed and after six of their returns.

Recent findings suggest that however, the patterns adopted afterward differed. Any lower-ranked bird was most often attacked after a top bird was removed. That result was recorded in five of the nine cases.

Bullying was recorded in eight of the nine cases after a top bird was returned.

On average, each of the 15 returning birds was the target of about 530 contests.

According to recent reports, those contests were counted over the three days after its return. Birds of similar rank had been targeted about 220 times over the three days before.

The flocks were not fighting more overall. About the same number of contests was recorded in each three-day period of the experiment. The birds had simply changed their targets.

“When removing a top-ranked bird, all the remaining birds have updated their rank in the other bird’s absence,” van der Marel said.

“And when the absent bird returns, the group shifts toward a bullying dominance pattern, maybe because they don’t want to lose their new rank position.”.

Returning top-ranked birds received much more aggression than returning lower-ranked birds did.

Sources indicate that the researchers compared responses by rank in the two flocks studied in 2022. Bullying was recorded in eight of 12 cases after a top bird was removed or returned.

The flock attacked any lower-ranked member in eight of 12 cases after a lower-ranked bird was removed or returned.

Removing a top-ranked bird also changes the flock’s mix of ranks. The experimental design therefore could not fully distinguish between two possible responses.

The flock may have reacted to the loss of that bird or to the new mix of ranks.

Memory may play a part, the authors suggested.

It has been revealed that earlier work by Hobson found strong evidence on this point. Monk parakeets remember whom they fought, who won, and how fights between other birds turned out.

Flock members that remember a former top bird may gain from bullying it, the authors wrote. Such bullying could stop the bird from retaking the top rank.

The authors also suggested that bullying could work as a signal to other birds that are watching.

According to recent reports, the birds were handled differently during removals and returns. The whole flock was netted and handled on removal days. Only the returning bird was handled on return days.

Recent findings suggest that the effect of handling could not be fully separated from the effect of the return, the authors wrote. They gave two reasons for thinking that handling was not the main cause.

According to recent reports, bullying was rarely recorded after the return of a lower-ranked bird. The storm and other unplanned events did not change the flock’s fighting pattern.

It has been revealed that the birds were also captive. Wild flocks of monk parakeets split apart and merge again often.

A wild flock can contain between one and 95 birds, and the average flock size is about four.

It has been revealed that A wild bird may be separated from its flockmates more often than the captive birds were. Those separations may also be shorter or longer than eight days.

What a flock or its members gain by switching patterns is still not known.

Industry observers note that the team is now splitting and merging flocks in ways closer to wild conditions. The fighting patterns of those flocks will then be checked for changes.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Computational Biology.

Lightning lights up towering storms above the South China Sea

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (796 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lightning illuminates towering thunderstorms over the South China Sea in an astronaut photo that also captures Singapore and fishing boat lights.
  • Today’s Image of the Day captures the South China Sea after dark, where city lights and scattered offshore glows surround towering thunderstorms.
  • Lightning briefly illuminates the clouds from within, revealing rounded storm tops that rise above the surrounding cloud cover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lightning illuminates towering thunderstorms over the South China Sea in an astronaut photo that also captures Singapore and fishing boat lights.

Today’s Image of the Day captures the South China Sea after dark, where city lights and scattered offshore glows surround towering thunderstorms.

Lightning briefly illuminates the clouds from within, revealing rounded storm tops that rise above the surrounding cloud cover.

These domes mark places where strong updrafts have pushed parts of the storms above their broad, flattened tops.

An astronaut aboard the International Space Station captured the scene near Borneo on October 28, 2026.

The photograph brings together several sources of nighttime light, each with a different explanation.

Recent findings suggest that thunderstorms begin with rising air. When warm, moist air moves upward, it cools, and water vapor condenses into cloud droplets.

With a continuing supply of moisture and upward motion, a cloud can grow into a towering storm.

Sources indicate that that growth eventually encounters an atmospheric boundary called the tropopause. It separates the troposphere, the lowest layer where most weather develops, from the stratosphere above.

It has been revealed that at this boundary, rising air generally spreads sideways. The result is the broad, flattened cloud canopy known as a thunderstorm’s anvil.

A particularly strong updraft can briefly push beyond that canopy, producing a rounded bulge called an overshooting top.

These protrusions reveal the force of the rising air inside a storm, even when much of its internal activity remains hidden.

Several overshooting tops appear in the astronaut’s photograph. Lightning illuminates two of them, helping expose their shapes against the dark surroundings.

Such domes can sometimes extend into the stratosphere.

Their presence signals vigorous storm development, although the photograph alone does not establish the precise height of these particular clouds.

The light inside a thunderstorm begins with interactions among tiny particles.

High in the cloud, rising air supports a mixture of ice crystals, supercooled water droplets, and soft ice pellets called graupel. Collisions among these particles transfer electrical charge.

The storm’s air currents help separate the charged particles.

Smaller ice crystals can travel upward, while heavier particles remain lower, allowing regions with different electrical charges to develop.

When the electrical field becomes strong enough, a lightning discharge occurs.

That discharge can remain inside a cloud or connect different clouds, rather than reaching the ground.

In a recent development, from below, an observer may see a branching bolt or a sudden brightening overhead. From orbit, clouds can scatter the light into a much broader glow.

The storm briefly reveals its contours, giving astronauts a view of cloud structure that people beneath it cannot see.

The photograph freezes one of those fleeting moments. It records the illuminated cloud tops alongside lights that were already shining across the surrounding land and sea.

Sources indicate that singapore appears on the left side of the image. The Singapore Strait separates the city-state from the Indonesian islands of Batam and Bintan to its south.

Elsewhere, clusters of light interrupt the darkness offshore.

NASA identifies the blue lights west of Singapore as likely fishing vessels using powerful lamps to attract squid or schooling fish, including anchovies and sardines.

Scattered orange points farther offshore to the northwest are likely gas flares.

Those identifications carry some uncertainty.

Color and location help interpret the scene, but a distant point of light does not reveal its source as clearly as a close-up photograph would.

Together, the lights show how much activity continues after sunset.

Urban areas form concentrated patches, while offshore operations produce isolated points and clusters across otherwise dark water.

The setting also helps explain why storms are a prominent part of the view.

According to recent reports, singapore experiences thunderstorms throughout the year. They become more frequent during the transition periods between monsoons, generally in April and May and again in October and November.

During these periods, light and variable winds favor the development of local thunderstorms, particularly during the afternoon and evening.

Warm, humid air supplies the ingredients for clouds to build upward.

This seasonal pattern provides context for the photograph, though it does not establish how each storm in the frame formed.

The image captures the region at 14:20 UTC, well after sunset locally. A member of the station’s Expedition 75 crew took the photo with a Nikon Z9 camera and a 14-millimeter lens.

The published photograph was cropped and enhanced for contrast, with lens artifacts removed.

For a moment, lightning made the atmosphere itself part of the illuminated landscape.

Beneath the station, the lights of a city, people working at sea, and towering tropical storms shared the same frame.

Sources indicate that image Credit: NASA/JSC, Expedition 75. Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-250951.

Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.
  • Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting tech giant in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

According to recent reports, the ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Recent findings suggest that joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

According to recent reports, the largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a significant hint, McConnell states, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”.

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”.

Industry observers note that based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Manufacturer was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Recent findings suggest that beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data revealed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell notes, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”.

In a recent development, these fresh findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”.

Industry News: These members of Congress are heading to the governor’s mansion

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The number of governors who once served in Congress is set to grow next year after several lawmakers won gubernatorial races across the country.
  • The incoming governors include members who’ve served in Congress for decades and some with relatively short stints in Congress.
  • Here are the lawmakers who won their governor’s races on election night:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The number of governors who once served in Congress is set to grow next year after several lawmakers won gubernatorial races across the country.

The incoming governors include members who’ve served in Congress for decades and some with relatively short stints in Congress. But several Republican lawmakers were unsuccessful in their attempts to become the top executives of their home states on what was largely a poor night for the GOP.

Here are the lawmakers who won their governor’s races on election night:.

Industry observers note that it was a blast from the (recent) past in Alabama, where Republican Sen. Tommy Tuberville was elected governor after defeating Democrat Doug Jones, his Senate predecessor whom he defeated in 2020.

Despite the defeat, Jones — who won a 2017 special election to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Alabama in more than two decades — lost by a closer-than-anticipated margin to Tuberville, a staunch ally of President Donald Trump and the former head football coach at Auburn. With 99 percent of votes counted, according to The Associated Press, Tuberville was leading Jones 52 percent to 48 percent — the narrowest gubernatorial race in the Yellowhammer State since 2002.

The governor’s mansion in the Sunshine State will remain in GOP hands, with Rep. Byron Donalds narrowly defeating former Rep. David Jolly to become Florida’s first Black governor.

Sources indicate that donalds, who was first elected to Congress in 2020, will succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, himself a former congressman.

Sources indicate that jolly is a former Republican lawmaker who left the party during Trump’s first term and joined Democrats last year. He was vying to become the first Democratic elected governor in Florida since Lawton Chiles won reelection in 1994. Jolly’s running mate was also a onetime House colleague — former Rep. Gwen Graham, the daughter of former Florida Gov. and Sen. Bob Graham.

The Volunteer State also made history on election night, electing its first female governor in Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn. Despite Tennessee’s deep-red lean, Blackburn only scraped by Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis City councilwoman, with a self-funding independent pulling in a portion of the conservative vote.

According to recent reports, before her election to the Senate in 2018, Blackburn served in the Tennessee Senate and nearly two decades in the House. She is expected to be able to pick her Senate successor after she is sworn in as governor.

According to recent reports, democratic-Farmer-Labor Sen. Amy Klobuchar was another history-maker in Minnesota, becoming the first female governor of the North Star State. She defeated Republican state House Speaker Lisa DeMuth in the race to succeed retiring Gov. Tim Walz, the 2024 Democratic vice presidential nominee.

Recent findings suggest that like Blackburn, Klobuchar was also the first woman to represent her state in the Senate, where she has served since 2007. She is also expected to appoint her successor in the chamber.

It has been revealed that unofficial returns from the U.S. Virgin Islands showed Democrat Stacey Plaskett prevailing in the open governor’s race with more than 50 percent of the vote to avoid a runoff and become the island territory’s first female governor.

Sources indicate that plaskett was first elected to Congress in 2014 as the Virgin Islands’ nonvoting delegate and served as a House impeachment manager during Trump’s second impeachment trial. She faced controversy last year over her correspondence with sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, but narrowly avoided being censured and stripped of her position on the House Intelligence Committee.

Two former members of Congress who later served in Joe Biden’s Cabinet are also heading for their states’ governor’s mansions.

In California, Democratic former Rep. Xavier Becerra easily defeated Republican Steve Hilton to succeed outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom. Since leaving Congress in 2017, Becerra has served as California attorney general and as Biden’s secretary of Health and Human Services.

And in Latest Mexico, former Rep. Deb Haaland easily kept the governorship in Democratic hands with her win over Republican Gregg Hull, the former Rio Rancho mayor. She succeeds another former House member, term-limited Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham.

Not all members of Congress were successful in governor’s races this year. A trio of Republican congressmen lost gubernatorial bids: Wisconsin’s Tom Tiffany, Arizona’s Andy Biggs and Michigan’s John James.

They join Republican colleagues who lost gubernatorial primaries this year, including David Schweikert of Arizona, Randy Feenstra of Iowa, Dusty Johnson of South Dakota, John W. Rose of Tennessee and Nancy Mace and Ralph Norman of South Carolina.

Sen. Michael Bennet, a Democrat from Colorado, lost a gubernatorial primary in June to state Attorney General Phil Weiser, who was easily elected Tuesday. Bennet, however, will continue to serve in the Senate as he isn’t up for reelection until 2028.

Andrew Menezes, Daniela Altimari, Mary Ellen McIntire and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

#30853. Bigger armies will not stop climate change, and may make the world less safe

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1304 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Bigger armies will not stop climate change, and may make the world less safe

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1304 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Military emissions stay out of national climate tallies, and two BMJ authors say bigger defense budgets may leave people less safe, not more.
  • Many governments are raising their military budgets, and climate change is now one of the reasons they give for doing so.
  • Two articles in a medical journal’s climate glitch say that logic has it backwards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Military emissions stay out of national climate tallies, and two BMJ authors say bigger defense budgets may leave people less safe, not more.

Many governments are raising their military budgets, and climate change is now one of the reasons they give for doing so. The thinking is that regions turning dangerously hot, wet, or dry will grow unstable and may go to war, so a bigger military is a precaution.

Two articles in a medical journal’s climate glitch say that logic has it backwards.

It has been revealed that war and the daily running of armies are themselves a large and mostly uncounted source of the gases heating the planet, their authors wrote. Spending more on them may leave people less safe, not more.

Industry observers note that the articles are opinion pieces, not data studies, and they appeared in The BMJ on October 21. Neta Crawford, a professor of international relations at the University of St Andrews, is the author of the first. The journal commissioned it and didn’t send it for outside peer review.

Recent findings suggest that mohammed Abba-Aji of Washington University in St. Louis and Nason Maani of the University of Edinburgh are the authors of the second article.

Recent findings suggest that in an interview with Earth.com, Abba-Aji described the comparison behind that article. “What struck me most was the contrast,” he mentioned. The contrast is between what the world spends on weapons and what it gives away as aid.

According to recent reports, security officials describe climate change as a “threat multiplier,” Crawford wrote. The phrase means a warming climate could stress societies until they fight. The U.S. military, the U.K. Ministry of Defence, NATO, and the U.N. Security Council have all used it.

Crawford reversed the claim: war, she wrote, is a climate change multiplier.

According to recent reports, the steadiest source of military emissions is the ordinary running of a military, from powering bases to the fuel burned in training and in moving troops. U.S. and NATO military doctrine stresses long-range air strikes, which produce more emissions than defensive doctrines do.

According to recent reports, everyday military emissions don’t appear in national greenhouse gas inventories. Crawford traced the gap to the Kyoto Protocol talks of the 1990s, when the U.S. Department of Defense pushed for a military exemption.

Recent findings suggest that the department was the country’s largest petroleum user and feared being required to cut its emissions. The Pentagon is still the largest user, she wrote, and its annual emissions are larger than those of most countries.

Industry observers note that arms makers add to the total. BAE Systems, the biggest defense manufacturer in the U.K., reported about 377,000 tons (341,686 metric tons) of carbon dioxide equivalent for 2025 from its own operations and purchased energy.

Recent findings suggest that fighting raises the numbers fast. Crawford cited an accounting group’s estimate for the first four years of the war in Ukraine. Military operations alone produced about 126 million tons (114 million metric tons) of emissions in the form of carbon dioxide equivalent.

Industry observers note that destroyed forests and airliners rerouted around the war zone added more, and rebuilding will add more again. Those three sources come to roughly 190 million tons (170 million metric tons).

It has been revealed that strikes on oil and gas sites are worse still. The Nord Stream pipelines under the Baltic Sea were sabotaged in September 2022, and an estimated 513,000 tons (465,000 metric tons) of methane escaped, a 2025 study published in Nature found.

Crawford put that at about 15 million tons (13.85 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide equivalent, three times what Albania emitted during the whole of 2024.

Ukrainian drones hit Russian oil facilities this September, Crawford wrote, and strikes hit oil and gas infrastructure in the Middle East during the war with Iran this year.

The fuel shortages and price jumps were tracked. In contrast, the greenhouse gases released have gone essentially uncounted.

The second article is about the money. World military spending reached $2,887 billion in 2025, Abba-Aji told Earth.com. This is close to 2.5 percent of everything the world’s economies produced.

Official development assistance, the aid that richer governments send to poorer ones, fell to $174 billion the same year, the largest one-year drop on record.

Abba-Aji and Maani describe a cycle. Climate stress can make conflict more likely, through competition over resources or by making it easier for armed groups to recruit.

“Conflict in turn justifies more military spending, and that spending draws money away from the measures that could break the cycle,” Abba-Aji said.

Wealthier governments may stay out of the fighting, the two wrote, and still help create the conditions for it. They supply the weapons that keep a conflict going while cutting aid to the countries affected.

It has been revealed that crawford also objects to the idea that a hotter world leads to war on its own. The link between climate change and armed conflict is neither strong nor necessary, she wrote, citing a 2017 study that re-examined the Syrian civil war.

Industry observers note that governments can support their populations instead, she wrote, and neighboring governments can negotiate over shared resources. Those are political choices, not unavoidable consequences of climate change.

In a recent development, climate change is already killing people without any war at all. In some regions, heatwaves, wildfires, storms, and floods made worse by warming now kill more people a year than armed conflict does, Crawford wrote.

By the Met Office‘s estimate, more than 1,100 deaths in England and Wales during the May and June heatwaves of 2026 were due to climate change.

According to recent reports, the threat-multiplier frame has also changed where militaries operate. For years, Crawford wrote, armed forces have worried that a melting Arctic Ocean will open shipping lanes and a contest for minerals.

The U.S., NATO, Russia, and China have all increased their Arctic operations, at the same time as the region’s climate has become less stable and those operations harder to run.

Sources indicate that some armed forces present themselves as green, Crawford wrote. The U.S. Navy publicized a “great green fleet” in 2016, and the U.S. Army promoted its investments in green technology until mention of climate change was all but banned under the Trump administration.

Sources indicate that moving bases off coal does cut emissions, she wrote. But even forces that use fuel-efficient vehicles, batteries, solar power, and microgrids remain major emitters.

When spending grows, so do training, operations, and purchasing, and the emissions grow with them.

“Substantial emission reductions will occur only when armed forces reduce their overall size and footprint and transition to lower emitting doctrines, including those that do not require long range aircraft missions,” Crawford wrote.

Asked by Earth.com what governments should do first, Abba-Aji mentioned they should “weigh the trade-offs between military and social spending for their health and climate consequences and set aside a share of security funding for climate adaptation, especially in the most vulnerable regions.”.

Crawford’s own answer is to spend more on health, the environment, and the energy transition rather than take money from them.

“While some form of defense is required, the focus should shift to how to ensure effective defense at lower emission levels and reduced costs,” she wrote.

According to recent reports, the size of the source that both articles describe is still unknown. Day-to-day military emissions are left out of national greenhouse gas inventories, and the gases released by this year’s strikes on oil and gas facilities haven’t been added up either.

Counting them would be the first step toward knowing its magnitude.

The full study was published in the journal The BMJ.

#30851. Uranus and Neptune’s strange magnetic fields may be getting stranger

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1164 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Uranus and Neptune’s strange magnetic fields may be getting stranger

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New simulations suggest Uranus and Neptune’s magnetic fields could shift dramatically within decades, driven by conditions deep inside the planets.
  • It has been revealed that earth’s magnetic field is fairly simple.
  • The magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune are far messier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New simulations suggest Uranus and Neptune’s magnetic fields could shift dramatically within decades, driven by conditions deep inside the planets.

It has been revealed that earth’s magnetic field is fairly simple. It has one strong north pole and one strong south pole, both lined up close to the axis the planet spins on, and that’s why a compass points north.

The magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune are far messier.

Both planets’ magnetic fields are strongly tilted relative to their rotation axes.

A newly introduced study suggests the reason lies deep inside both planets, and that their fields may look quite different today from the last time a spacecraft measured them.

In a recent development, the study focuses on how well material deep inside the planets conducts electricity. In the computer models, conductivity increased with depth.

With that one change, the simulated fields matched the broad features measured during Voyager 2’s flybys in the 1980s.

The work was led by Chi Yan, a research associate at the Jackson School of Geosciences at The University of Texas at Austin.

Yan’s study is built on simulations, not new measurements. Each planet’s magnetic field has been measured up close only once.

According to recent reports, NASA’s Voyager 2 flew past Uranus in 1986 and past Neptune in 1989. It’s still the only spacecraft to have visited either planet.

Earth’s magnetic field is tilted about 11 degrees from the axis it spins around. Voyager 2 found that Uranus’ field is tilted 59 degrees and Neptune’s is tilted 47 degrees.

The tilt isn’t the only odd part.

On every other planet with a known magnetic field, the simple north-south pattern accounts for 74% to 98% of the magnetic energy at the surface.

For Uranus and Neptune, the figure is only 12%. The rest of their magnetic energy comes from smaller, more complicated patterns.

Industry observers note that A planet makes a magnetic field when fluid that can carry electric current moves around deep inside it. Scientists call this process a dynamo.

Earth’s outer core is liquid iron, surrounded by a mostly solid layer of rock. As the molten iron moves, shaped by Earth’s spin, it produces a field with strong north and south poles.

Uranus and Neptune are about four times wider than Earth.

Scientists think they are made mostly of hydrogen, helium, water, ammonia, methane and rocky material, though the exact makeup is still unknown.

They’re called ice giants because water, ammonia and methane are classified as ices in planetary science.

According to recent reports, yan noted the planets’ large size and chemistry could explain the tilted fields. Under enough pressure, water molecules can split into charged pieces called ions, which let electricity flow.

“Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high,” noted Yan.

“Under these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.”.

The researchers simulated fluid moving inside an ice giant and tracked how the flow, the heat and the magnetic field changed together.

The team tested several interior layouts, with thicker and thinner layers of moving fluid.

In some runs, the fluid conducted electricity equally well at every depth. Those runs made strong, upright fields much like Earth’s, and the poles never flipped.

According to recent reports, when the fluid conducted better with depth, the result changed in every layout the team tried. The fields became messy, with several poles, and they flipped direction at irregular times.

Recent findings suggest that near the top of the moving layer, where the fluid conducted less well, magnetic forces had less control over the flow. The motion there broke into smaller, more vigorous swirls.

According to recent reports, the runs that looked most like Uranus and Neptune had a fairly thin layer of moving fluid. The authors wrote that the effect doesn’t need finely tuned conditions.

That flexibility matters because the two planets differ sharply in heat.

Uranus gives off little heat beyond the sunlight it absorbs. Neptune gives off nearly twice the energy it receives from the Sun.

In two runs, the simulated fields closely resembled those measured at Uranus and Neptune, then looked clearly different 32 simulated years later.

More than 30 years have passed since Voyager 2’s visits.

“Earth’s magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years,” said Yan.

According to recent reports, “Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.”.

According to recent reports, in one run that resembled Uranus, the tilt moved 84 degrees over 40 years. In another, it moved 13 degrees. Fast and slow change both showed up in runs resembling Uranus.

A 13-degree shift would fit what telescopes have seen at Uranus. Its auroras have appeared in roughly the same places as in 1986, give or take 10 to 20 degrees.

The slow periods didn’t last, though. In the 13-degree run, the field soon started changing faster.

Auroras are one way to check. They form when charged particles from the Sun interact with gases high in a planet’s atmosphere, and where they show up can hint at whether the planet’s magnetic tilt has moved.

Some recent telescope studies, including one that estimated Uranus’ rotation rate by tracking its auroras, assumed its magnetic field had remained unchanged since 1986.

At Neptune, the southern aurora appears to have moved about 30 degrees in latitude between 1989 and 2023.

Researchers aren’t sure yet whether that move reflects a change in the magnetic field.

They are now studying sharp infrared images of both planets’ auroras from the James Webb Space Telescope.

Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University, led that observing campaign and reviewed the new paper for the journal.

Both planets also have an ionosphere, an electrically charged layer high in the atmosphere.

“We are busy working on what’s contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an important stepping stone,” mentioned Stallard.

Yan’s group plans to combine the Webb aurora images, Voyager 2’s magnetic readings and the simulations to estimate how the two fields are arranged today.

Uranus’ magnetic field could also turn out to change slowly over a long period.

If it does, the models suggest the planet’s deep interior carries electricity about 10 times better than standard estimates.

That could mean the inside of Uranus is hotter than scientists thought. Or it could mean the interior holds materials that carry electricity more easily.

Understanding the interiors properly will take new missions back to the ice giants, the researchers wrote.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Physics.

Breaking: Science to restore speech is moving fast. Here’s what’s next

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists are racing to restore people’s ability to communicate.
  • This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me takes listeners through the breadth of scientific efforts to restore words, emotions and even gestures to people who can’t move or talk.
  • Sources indicate that we’ll hear from Casey Harrell, a man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis who can no longer talk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clouds block satellite cameras, so an AI learned how to redraw the ground beneath them

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GeoCore-9B learned how to recreate the ground that is hidden beneath cloud cover in satellite photos.
  • Industry observers note that A satellite picture of a flooded town is only worth something if the camera can see the town.
  • It was built to know where on Earth it is looking and how much ground each pixel covers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GeoCore-9B learned how to recreate the ground that is hidden beneath cloud cover in satellite photos.

Industry observers note that A satellite picture of a flooded town is only worth something if the camera can see the town. On a cloudy day it can’t, and the picture highlights cloud where the streets should be. A fresh AI model fills those streets back in.

It was built to know where on Earth it is looking and how much ground each pixel covers.

In a recent development, jeonghyeok Do and Munchurl Kim of KAIST in South Korea built the model, called GeoCore-9B. Their paper is a preprint that has been accepted for presentation at NeurIPS 2026, an artificial intelligence conference. It has not yet been published in a journal.

Sources indicate that the ground the model draws under a cloud is a reconstruction, not a photograph. Do and Kim make that point themselves, and they warn that realistic fake satellite imagery could be used to spread disinformation about disasters or geopolitical events.

Ordinary satellite pictures work like a camera. They record sunlight bouncing off the ground, so thick cloud or nighttime leaves them with nothing to record.

That matters most during floods and wildfires, when the weather is often bad and the ground is exactly what people need to see.

A radar satellite sends radio waves down and measures the echoes that come back. The method is called synthetic aperture radar, and it works at night and through cloud.

But its images don’t look like photographs, because brightness and texture in them mean different things. Do and Kim wanted one model for both problems.

It has been revealed that earlier attempts started with an AI built to generate ordinary photographs and then taught it about satellites. Do and Kim wrote that this builds in biases.

Ordinary photos are taken from eye level with a subject in the middle, while a satellite looks straight down at a scene with no center.

So they trained their AI model from scratch on satellite views alone, adjusting about 9 billion internal settings, known as parameters, as it learned.

According to recent reports, the training set was 10 million satellite images, each paired with a sentence describing it. The note for a port mentioned ships and warehouses; the note for farmland mentioned a road between fields.

Each image also carried its latitude, longitude, and how much ground one pixel covers. A building looks very different when each pixel covers about 3 feet (1 meter) than when each covers about 105 feet (32 meters).

Without that number, a small building and a large industrial plant can have the same shape.

In a recent development, A model this large, trained from nothing, learns slowly and tends to produce scenes with no coherent layout. So Do and Kim brought in a second AI, already trained to recognize satellite imagery, as a teacher.

During training, the newly introduced model was scored on how well its internal picture of a scene agreed with the teacher’s picture of how roads connect and where field boundaries lie.

The teacher is switched off once training ends, so it adds no work when the model is in use. Without it, the team found, the model’s images had fragmented textures and distorted structures. With it, every score they tracked improved.

Recent findings suggest that the team also tested what the model had absorbed about geography. Given only a latitude and longitude, with no text at all, it drew dense skyscrapers for the coordinates of New York City and ice fields for Antarctica. It drew sand dunes for the Sahara and forest for the Amazon.

The team checked 500 of these coordinate-only images generated by the model against all 10.5 million real world photos that were used as training images.

They found none that closely matched the real-world satellite images, suggesting that the AI was not simply copying existing photographs. However, they wrote that the test can’t rule out every form of memorization used by the AI model.

It has been revealed that to put the model to work, Do and Kim froze it and trained a small set of extra settings for each task. This was far cheaper than retraining it.

According to recent reports, on a public test set of cloudy and clear image pairs, GeoCore-9B outscored every program built specifically for cloud removal on two of three standard measures. Those were cover brightness and color accuracy, and how closely the structure matches the clear image.

On the third, how natural the image looks, it scored about the same as the best specialist. The roads and field boundaries in its reconstructions stayed where the clear images put them.

It has been revealed that on a second public dataset, the model turned radar images into photo-like images. It scored best on the two measures of realism and fine detail, and it roughly matched the best specialist on structural similarity.

“By training the AI on where each satellite image was taken and the actual size of the terrain it demonstrates, we made it possible to use a single model for multiple tasks such as cloud removal and image conversion,” mentioned Kim, a professor in KAIST’s School of Electrical Engineering.

He added that he expects the work to make weather-limited satellite data more usable for assessing disasters and monitoring changes in forests and cities.

Sources indicate that the model only produces ordinary color images. It can read a radar image but can’t generate one. In addition, it doesn’t handle the multispectral images, with light bands beyond visible color, that some Earth-observation satellites record.

According to recent reports, one piece, the component that compresses each image before the model works on it, came from ordinary photography. On the cloud-removal images, it kept the main features but lost some faint local detail.

By their own account, the experiments can’t say how much of the gain came from the model’s size, its training data, or the teacher.

Recent findings suggest that so far each task has been tested on a single public dataset. How the model performs on other satellites and regions is unknown, and that is the test Do and Kim plan next.

Industry observers note that do and Kim also want the model to predict changes on the ground: flooding, building damage, wildfire spread, and urban growth. The team intends to explore surveillance and reconnaissance as well.

The model’s code and weights are online, so other groups can run those tests.

The full study has been posted as a preprint on arXiv and accepted for presentation at NeurIPS 2026. It has not been published in a journal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek to serve as House minority leader in the next Congress.

A source familiar with the speaker’s decision confirmed that the Louisiana Republican would not seek the post after Tuesday’s midterm elections saw Republicans lose their narrow majority in a Democratic tsunami.

Other candidates were already lining up. Fellow Louisiana Republican Steve Scalise, the current majority leader, is expected to launch a bid for minority leader Wednesday, according to a person familiar with his plans who described him as a “proven and tested leader.” And House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio is also throwing in his hat, according to multiple reports.

The Republican conference is set to hold its leadership elections next week.

Johnson held an election night event in Shreveport, La., after crisscrossing the country trying to protect the GOP majority, arguing throughout the campaign that polling favoring Democrats would not be accurate.

“While the outcome of this midterm is not what we’d hoped and fought for, a upcoming battle is just beginning. This Democrat House majority will be led by the most radical and extreme leftists in American history,” Johnson remarked in a statement after Democrats claimed the majority. “However, Republicans will never stop fighting to defend the Constitution and protect the foundations that have made America the greatest nation in the history of the world.”.

The blame game had already begun Wednesday morning, as Republicans reeled from losses that cut deeper than expected.

Sources indicate that “The polls were not wrong. You were,” Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., wrote on social media, referring to his party’s leaders in the House and Senate. “Please do us all a favor and step aside so new leadership can take a truly conservative direction.”.

#30844. Latest Update: New hypothesis explains why the right side of the human brain controls the left side of the body

Latest Update: New hypothesis explains why the right side of the human brain controls the left side of the body

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The brain's crossed wiring runs through every vertebrate group, and two neuroscientists trace it to the eyes of the first fishes.
  • A stroke on the right side of the brain weakens the left arm and leg.
  • It has been revealed that two neuroscientists have traced the crossing through every major group of living vertebrates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brain's crossed wiring runs through every vertebrate group, and two neuroscientists trace it to the eyes of the first fishes.

A stroke on the right side of the brain weakens the left arm and leg. The brain is cross-wired that way, and for more than a century scientists have assumed there was an evolutionary reason for it.

It has been revealed that two neuroscientists have traced the crossing through every major group of living vertebrates. They now propose that evolution may never have selected it for the jobs it does.

On their reading, the crossed wiring may simply be inherited from the way the first fishes’ eyes were wired to their brains, some 500 million years ago.

Martin Wessendorf, an associate professor emeritus of neuroscience at the University of Minnesota, and Daniel Wang, a researcher in the University’s Department of Neuroscience, wrote the review.

It is a hypothesis built from more than a century of published anatomy rather than a new experiment. However, the authors wrote that it may be testable in fossils.

In an interview with Earth.com, Wang said the question reaches beyond his own field.

“This’ll be relevant to anyone who wants to know more about why brain injury on one side of the head often leads to loss of function on the opposite side of the body,” he said.

The crossing begins at the eye. The lens flips the image, so whatever sits to your right lands on the left side of each retina. The nerve fibers carrying the right half of the view then sort themselves at a junction behind the eyes and run to the left side of the brain.

According to recent reports, one place that information goes is a structure in the midbrain called the optic tectum. It holds a map of the opposite half of visual space, and it fires fast turning and escape movements.

Every vertebrate examined appears to have one, lampreys and hagfish included, along with the crossing junction behind the eyes.

Living jawless fish carry both, so the authors conclude that the last common ancestor of all vertebrates probably did too. That puts the first crossed wiring in the Cambrian period, among jawless fishes that lived roughly 538 to 486 million years ago.

Anatomists call crossed wiring contralateral organization, and its age is what struck Wang.

“What surprised me the most was likely just how old the contralateral organization of the optic tectum is for vertebrates – spanning even to the Cambrian,” he told Earth.com.

Body senses crossed next. Two pathways carry touch, pain, temperature and body position from the spinal cord up to the brain, and both cross the midline in amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

The one for light touch and body position is missing in fishes, so the authors trace it to the last common ancestor of the four-limbed animals.

In a recent development, movement pathways cross too. One runs from the optic tectum down to the spinal cord and turns the body toward whatever just appeared at the edge of vision.

Lampreys and bony fish appear to have no such pathway. Sharks have one that mostly stays on its own side, and rays and lungfish have a crossed one.

Recent findings suggest that reptiles appear to have lost that pathway. A second crossed pathway, from a cluster of midbrain cells called the red nucleus, is thought to help control limbs.

True mammals appeared about 165 million years ago. By then, those crossed senses and movement pathways had already existed for almost 200 million years.

According to recent reports, the pathway that lets you move one finger at a time is the special case. It runs from the cerebral cortex, the six-layered outer sheet found only in mammals, down to the spinal cord, and it crosses in the lower brainstem.

In most mammals, it ends where touch signals enter the cord and adjusts those signals. Few mammals besides primates, raccoons and kinkajous have a version that reaches the nerve cells that drive muscles.

In a recent development, so the circuit that gives humans fine control of their hands appears to be a sensory circuit put to a new use. Wang said that was the finding that surprised his co-author most.

“This demonstrates that circuitry that’s involved in one function can, with just a change or two, become a function that’s entirely different.”.

In a recent development, the crossing isn’t universal in this pathway. In goats and elephants, it runs down both sides of the spinal cord, and in hedgehogs and moles it mostly stays on its own side. Even in humans, an estimated 10 to 25 percent of its fibers don’t cross.

It has been revealed that wang pointed to the goats and elephants, “so there’s a decent amount of diversity there,” he noted. The authors read that variety as a sign that natural selection wasn’t strongly favoring the crossing in this pathway.

Isaac Newton proposed in 1704 that the junction behind the eyes sorts nerve fibers by visual field.

Recent findings suggest that ramón y Cajal, who later won a Nobel Prize for his work on the structure of the nervous system, went further in an 1898 paper. Once the visual map crossed, he proposed, it would pay for the maps of hearing, touch and movement to match it.

In computer models published in 2014, an animal controlled by the opposite side of its brain was likelier to survive a blow to one side of the head or body.

According to recent reports, at least two other research groups have blamed a twist in the body plan, dating to the split between vertebrates and their invertebrate ancestors. That argument goes back to an 1822 dissection of a crayfish.

The authors see a problem with the twist. The visual system was probably crossed in the first vertebrates, but the pathways for touch, limb control and finger control didn’t exist yet.

So the authors doubt that a single ancient twist can explain them.

The authors’ own answer starts with the optic tectum. Its map of the opposite half of visual space sits on top. Beneath it, in register, sit maps of touch and hearing from the same half, and at the bottom sit the cells that fire movements.

Wessendorf and Wang propose that this stack biased the sensory and motor pathways that evolved later toward crossing.

According to recent reports, when the cortex evolved, most of the pathways carrying signals into it were already crossed. A cortex wired to its own side would have needed extra crossings to collect vision, touch and hearing from the far side, or a rewiring of every older circuit.

The authors argue that either change would have carried a “wiring cost,” leaving mammals that were less energy-efficient, less intelligent, or both.

Recent findings suggest that not everything crosses. Smell and taste mostly stay on the same side, and the authors note that neither sense maps space the way vision, hearing and touch do.

The cerebellum, which coordinates movement, works the same side of the body it sits on.

“We propose that contralateral organization didn’t necessarily evolve as an adaptation, but because evolution is an engineer that builds with the foundation and materials it has at hand,” Wang and Wessendorf wrote.

According to recent reports, the authors list what would test the idea. Their first prediction is that the last common ancestor of vertebrates had both the crossing junction and an optic tectum.

Cambrian fossils of jawless fish exist, and a fossilized brain cast from one could show whether both were there.

Wang remarked the finding that would complicate the idea is an early fossil vertebrate whose optic tectum handled vision on the same side rather than the opposite one.

According to recent reports, the authors also predict that crossed pathways from the forebrain to the spinal cord will prove widespread in birds. Unfortunately, relatively few bird species have been examined.

Crocodilians appear not to have been checked, and the authors predict they have one too.

According to recent reports, hearing is the one sense the authors treat with caution. It appears to have evolved partly on its own in different lines.

What remains unknown is whether any Cambrian fish skull preserves enough of its brain to show the crossing.

Industry observers note that until one does, the idea rests on living anatomy. The next checks are in the fossil record, and in the birds and crocodilians whose spinal pathways have yet to be mapped.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Neuroanatomy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover.

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of Fresh York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani states gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

It has been revealed that to design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”.
